data.title: mTORC1 and mTORC2 selectively regulate CD8+ T cell differentiation
data.authors: Pollizzi KN; Patel CH; Sun IH; Oh MH; Waickman AT; Wen J; Delgoffe GM; Powell JD

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Mice with T-cell-specific deletion of Tsc2, Rheb or Rictor (and Tsc2/Rictor double knockout), OT-I adoptive transfer, vaccinia-OVA and Listeria-OVA infection, EL4 and B16-OVA tumour models, rapamycin (100 ug/kg/day) and 2-deoxyglucose in vivo, Seahorse metabolic profiling
data.finding: By deleting Tsc2, Rheb or Rictor in T cells, this work split the CD8 response between the two mTOR complexes. Tsc2 loss left mTORC1 constitutively active: the cells were strongly glycolytic (high ECAR, high Slc2a1 and Pfk1, low spare respiratory capacity), made more IFN-gamma, TNF and granzyme B, cleared EL4 thymoma and slowed B16-OVA growth, but stayed terminally differentiated and were about two-fold fewer than wild type at day 30, with no memory. Rheb loss removed mTORC1 activity with mTORC2 intact: those cells failed as effectors but kept memory-like features and were about two-fold more numerous at day 30, yet did not respond to rechallenge, which the authors trace to metabolic defects. Rapamycin from day 5 (100 ug/kg daily) rescued survival of Tsc2-deficient cells, raised CD127 and Eomesodermin, lowered KLRG1 and T-bet and restored a recall response. Losing mTORC2 by Rictor deletion left effector function intact but increased memory cells that still responded 133 days after infection, and the Tsc2/Rictor double knockout showed that the hyperactive effector phenotype needs mTORC2. Boundary: mouse genetics with TCR-transgenic transfers and transplantable tumours; the comparison rests on genetic extremes (no TSC2, no Rheb, no Rictor) rather than graded physiological signalling, and nothing here is measured in people.

data.title: Rapamycin inhibits the secretory phenotype of senescent cells by a Nrf2-independent mechanism
data.authors: Wang Rong; Yu Z; Sunchu B; Shoaf J; Dang I; Zhao S; Caples K; Bradley L; Beaver LM; Ho E; Löhr CV; Perez VI

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Mouse skin fibroblasts and WT vs Nrf2-knockout MEFs (H2O2- or bleomycin-induced senescence); human WI38 fibroblasts (replicative senescence, CRISPR Nrf2 knockout); WT and Nrf2-knockout mice given rapamycin 4 mg/kg i.p. every other day for 6 weeks
data.finding: The authors asked whether the transcription factor Nrf2 is needed for rapamycin to hold back cellular senescence. In wild-type mouse fibroblasts exposed to hydrogen peroxide, rapamycin raised Nrf2, switched on autophagy and lowered the senescence markers p16 and p21, beta-galactosidase staining and the inflammatory secretory profile (SASP). In Nrf2-knockout cells rapamycin still lowered beta-galactosidase staining and the SASP, but no longer lowered p16 and p21 or activated autophagy; re-expressing Nrf2 restored those effects, and human WI38 cells with Nrf2 knocked out by CRISPR behaved the same way. In Nrf2-knockout mice given rapamycin (4 mg/kg every other day for 6 weeks, 8 mice per group), fat-tissue beta-galactosidase staining and pro-inflammatory cytokines fell while p16 did not, and rapamycin lowered STAT3 phosphorylation in lung tissue and WI38 cells. The study provided evidence that rapamycin's effect on the SASP can be separated from its Nrf2-dependent effect on cell-cycle arrest. Boundary: Mouse and human fibroblasts in culture plus a short 6-week dosing study in young Nrf2-knockout mice; mTOR inhibition was by rapamycin, which was given before and during the senescence trigger, so this is prevention of senescence onset rather than treatment of established senescent cells.

data.title: NUFIP1 is a ribosome receptor for starvation-induced ribophagy
data.authors: Wyant GA; Abu-Remaileh M; Frenkel EM; Laqtom NN; Dharamdasani V; Lewis CA; Chan SH; Heinze I; Ori A; Sabatini DM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: HEK-293T and other human/mouse cell lines (incl. 8988T); LysoIP lysosome proteomics; CRISPR knockouts of NUFIP1, ATG7, DEPDC5 (GATOR1); Torin1, amino-acid and glucose starvation; electron microscopy
data.finding: The authors purified lysosomes from human cells and measured how their protein content changes when mTORC1 is switched off by nutrient starvation or by the mTOR inhibitor Torin1, defining 828 lysosome-associated proteins. One responder, NUFIP1 (with its partner ZNHIT3), moved from the nucleus to autophagosomes and lysosomes after mTORC1 inhibition, bound ribosomes from Torin1-treated cells, and bound LC3B directly through a motif lost in the W40A mutant. Without NUFIP1 or its LC3B-binding ability, starvation or Torin1 no longer depleted ribosomal proteins and rRNA, while bulk autophagy and ferritin degradation were unaffected. In cells lacking the GATOR1 subunit DEPDC5, where mTORC1 ignores amino-acid loss, starvation no longer depleted ribosomal proteins but Torin1 still did, which points to mTORC1 inhibition as the trigger. NUFIP1 loss reduced survival under starvation (rescued by nucleosides) and blunted mTORC1 reactivation after long arginine deprivation. Boundary: Human and mouse cell lines over hours of starvation; Torin1 inhibits both mTOR complexes. No tissue or whole-animal data.

data.title: Lysosomal GPCR-like protein LYCHOS signals cholesterol sufficiency to mTORC1
data.authors: Shin HR; Citron YR; Wang L; Tribouillard L; Goul CS; Stipp R; Sugasawa Y; Jain A; Samson N; Lim CY; Davis OB; Castaneda-Carpio D; Qian M; Nomura DK; Perera RM; Park E; Covey DF; Laplante M; Evers AS; Zoncu R

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human cell lines (HEK293T, lysosomal proteomics); cholesterol-binding and GATOR1-binding assays
data.finding: Identifies LYCHOS (previously annotated GPR155) as a lysosomal cholesterol sensor for mTORC1. Cholesterol binds the amino-terminal permease-like region; mutating that site impairs mTORC1 activation. At high cholesterol LYCHOS binds GATOR1 through a conserved cytoplasm-facing loop, and by sequestering GATOR1 it promotes cholesterol- and Rag-dependent recruitment of mTORC1 to the lysosome. Boundary: human cell lines and biochemistry, not an organismal phenotype.

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.authors: Esposito A; Bayramoglu I; Varriale C; Cavaliere MP; Brunetti ME; Agostinis R; Jansen RM; Tudorica DA; Duan Y; Spacci M; Calcagnì A; Strobl CD; Passerini V; Andreone F; Monfregola J; Richter J; Sacco F; Klapper W; Weigert O; Ballabio A; Zoncu R; Hurley JH; Dengjel J; Napolitano G

data.title: mTORC1 stimulates cell growth through SAM synthesis and m6A mRNA-dependent control of protein synthesis
data.authors: Villa E; Sahu U; O'Hara BP; Ali ES; Helmin KA; Asara JM; Gao P; Singer BD; Ben-Sahra I

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: SAMTOR (GU2017) showed the cell can sense S-adenosylmethionine and report it to mTORC1. This study runs the arrow the other way: mTORC1 controls how much SAM the cell makes. Downstream of mTORC1, c-MYC binds intron 1 of MAT2A and raises expression of the enzyme that produces SAM, the cell's main methyl donor; mTORC1 separately increases the protein level of WTAP, the regulatory subunit of the m6A RNA methyltransferase complex. Together these raise m6A methylation of mRNA, which primes the translation machinery for growth. Blocking MAT2A lowers SAM, m6A, protein synthesis rate and tumor growth.

data.title: Lysosomal positioning coordinates cellular nutrient responses
data.authors: Korolchuk VI; Saiki S; Lichtenberg M; Siddiqi FH; Roberts EA; Imarisio S; Jahreiss L; Sarkar S; Futter M; Menzies FM; O'Kane CJ; Deretic V; Rubinsztein DC

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Where the lysosome sits inside the cell helps decide whether mTORC1 is on. With nutrients available, lysosomes move to the cell periphery, physically close to the plasma-membrane signalling modules, and mTORC1 is active there; starvation changes intracellular pH and pulls lysosomes into a cluster around the nucleus, where mTORC1 output falls and autophagy is released. Lysosomal position also sets the rate of autophagosome-lysosome fusion, so one variable acts at both the initiation and the termination end of autophagic flux. This added a spatial axis to mTORC1 regulation that Rag/Ragulator recruitment alone does not account for.

data.title: Regulation of TFEB and V-ATPases by mTORC1
data.authors: Peña-Llopis S; Vega-Rubin-de-Celis S; Schwartz JC; Wolff NC; Tran TA; Zou L; Xie XJ; Corey DR; Brugarolas J

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Tsc2-/- vs Tsc2+/+ immortalized MEFs (serum-deprived, +/- rapamycin) with microarrays; Tsc1 floxed primary MEFs and mouse liver (Ad-Cre); myr-Akt prostate model with everolimus (public data); HeLa cells with TSC2/Raptor knockdown
data.finding: Using Tsc2-null and wild-type mouse fibroblasts with and without rapamycin, the authors looked for genes whose expression follows mTORC1 activity and found 75 genes, enriched for subunits of the lysosomal proton pump (V-ATPase). mTORC1 also raised V-ATPase expression in mouse liver after Tsc1 deletion and in a prostate tumour model, through a transcriptional mechanism that needed the transcription factor TFEB: knocking down Tfeb cut the number of mTORC1-induced genes from 1146 to 424 probes, and about a quarter of mTORC1-induced genes depended on Tfeb. mTORC1 promoted albumin uptake (endocytosis) in a Tfeb- and V-ATPase-dependent way. In these serum-deprived cells, active mTORC1 (TSC loss) increased nuclear TFEB and rapamycin or Raptor knockdown reduced it, which is the opposite direction to the TFEB inhibition reported by later studies in fed or starved cells. Boundary: Mostly mouse and human cell lines under low serum; liver and prostate data are expression measurements. The direction of mTORC1 control over TFEB localisation here differs from later work and is condition-dependent.

data.authors: Bobok N

evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.title: ERK2 phosphorylates PFAS to mediate posttranslational control of de novo purine synthesis
data.authors: Ali ES; Sahu U; Villa E; O'Hara BP; Gao P; Beaudet C; Wood AW; Asara JM; Ben-Sahra I

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: The Atlas records several routes by which mTORC1 drives purine synthesis. This study shows mTORC1 is not the only growth pathway with that power: RAS-ERK signalling stimulates purine synthesis directly and within minutes, because ERK2 - but not ERK1 - phosphorylates the purine synthesis enzyme PFAS at Thr619. Cells expressing a PFAS that cannot be phosphorylated make fewer purines, form fewer colonies and grow smaller tumors. Two points bound the mTOR claim: the control is posttranslational, so it acts far faster than transcription or translation, and it is a parallel input, so purine synthesis in a RAS-driven tumor is not read out from mTORC1 activity alone.

data.title: Autism-related deficits via dysregulated eIF4E-dependent translational control
data.authors: Gkogkas CG; Khoutorsky A; Ran I; Rampakakis E; Nevarko T; Weatherill DB; Vasuta C; Yee S; Truitt M; Dallaire P; Major F; Lasko P; Ruggero D; Nader K; Lacaille JC; Sonenberg N

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Eif4ebp2 knockout mice and betaT-Eif4e (eIF4E-overexpressing) mice; hippocampal slices and slice cultures; MEF reporter assays; icv 4EGI-1 and lentiviral shRNA
data.finding: Mice lacking 4E-BP2, the main brain brake on eIF4E downstream of mTORC1, showed autism-like behaviours: reduced social approach in the three-chamber test, more self-grooming and marble burying, and more ultrasonic calls as pups. Polysome profiling of hippocampus showed that, of 24 autism-linked mRNAs tested, only the neuroligin 1-4 mRNAs shifted to heavier polysomes in the knockout, with no change in their mRNA levels or in global protein synthesis; eIF4E-overexpressing mice showed the same neuroligin shift. Knockout neurons had larger excitatory than inhibitory synaptic charge transfer, raising the excitation/inhibition ratio. Five days of brain infusion of 4EGI-1, which blocks eIF4E binding to eIF4G, brought cap-bound eIF4E/eIF4G and neuroligin levels back to normal and reversed the social deficit, and knocking down neuroligin 1 (but not neuroligin 2) partly restored social behaviour. Boundary: mouse genetic models (male mice for behaviour); mTOR itself was not manipulated; the link to human autism is by analogy.

data.title: Drosophila S6 kinase: a regulator of cell size
data.authors: Montagne J; Stewart MJ; Stocker H; Hafen E; Kozma SC; Thomas G

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Drosophila melanogaster dS6K-deficient mutants; mosaic (clonal) analysis of wing and larval cells
data.finding: The authors made fruit flies lacking the S6 kinase gene (dS6K) and followed their development. These flies developed with a strong delay and ended up much smaller. The smaller body came from smaller cells, not from fewer cells. The effect was cell-autonomous, seen across larval development, and differed from the phenotype of ribosomal protein (Minute) mutants. The authors concluded that S6K controls cell size in flies without changing cell number. Boundary: Drosophila only; genetic loss of S6K from the start of development, so it does not show what happens when S6K is lowered in adult animals or in mammals.

data.title: Tsc tumour suppressor proteins antagonize amino-acid-TOR signalling
data.authors: Gao X; Zhang Y; Arrazola P; Hino O; Kobayashi T; Yeung RS; Ru B; Pan D

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Drosophila melanogaster genetics (Tsc1/Tsc2 mutants); Tsc-deficient mammalian cells
data.finding: The authors asked how the Tsc1 and Tsc2 tumour suppressors relate to TOR, the nutrient-sensing kinase. They showed that Tsc1 and Tsc2 can physically associate with TOR and act upstream of TOR in fly genetic tests. In fly and mammalian cells lacking Tsc1 or Tsc2, S6K activity rose, and this increase depended on TOR. S6K normally switches off when cells are starved of amino acids, but cells without Tsc1-Tsc2 stayed resistant to that starvation. The authors proposed that the Tsc1-Tsc2 complex restrains the TOR response to amino acids. Boundary: Drosophila and cultured mammalian cells; S6K activity is used as the readout of TOR. Later work placed amino acid sensing mainly on the Rag GTPase arm rather than through TSC, so the amino acid part of the model is not the current consensus.

In fruit flies expressing wild-type or mutant human tau, rapamycin reduced tau toxicity, and this went with less insoluble tau. The authors argued that inducing autophagy with rapamycin could be useful across several aggregate-prone protein diseases, not only Huntington's disease. data.authors: Majumder S; Caccamo A; Medina DX; Benavides AD; Javors MA; Kraig E; Strong R; Richardson A; Oddo S

evidence.label: Animal model

data.finding: Mice were fed rapamycin in their food either from 2 months of age or only from 15 months, when age-related memory deficits were already present, and all were tested at 18 months in a water maze (20 mice per group). Boundary: Mice of one mixed strain, normal ageing (not an Alzheimer model); the late-start arm showed no reversal of existing deficits, and the IL-1beta and NMDA links are correlations, not tested by blocking them.

data.title: Alternative rapamycin treatment regimens mitigate the impact of rapamycin on glucose homeostasis and the immune system
data.authors: Arriola Apelo SI; Neuman JC; Baar EL; Syed FA; Cummings NE; Brar HK; Pumper CP; Kimple ME; Lamming DW

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Mice given rapamycin every day (2 mg/kg) developed glucose intolerance (the glucose curve was about 71% higher), raised fasting glucose and insulin, and their pancreatic islets released less insulin. The same dose given once every 5 days did not impair glucose tolerance or insulin tolerance, and fasting glucose and insulin stayed normal. Dosing every 3 days was already too frequent. Pyruvate tolerance, a liver measure, was still impaired, about half as much as with daily dosing. The drug is cleared within about a week (blood half-life roughly 15 hours), so mTORC1 was not blocked continuously. The immune effect got smaller but did not disappear (regulatory T cells fell about 25% versus about 60% on daily dosing), and testis weight still dropped by about 60% versus 75 to 80%. Everolimus and temsirolimus blocked mTORC1 as well as rapamycin but disturbed glucose tolerance less. Boundary: young male mice treated for 2 to 8 weeks, side effects only. No lifespan or benefit was measured, so this shows that harm can be reduced, not that the benefit is kept (see ARR2016 and BIT2016).

evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Female 129/Sv inbred mice received rapamycin intermittently, 2 weeks in every month, from 2 months of age for the rest of their lives. Treated mice gained less weight with age, showed a slower estimated rate of ageing, lived longer, with the gain most visible among the last survivors, and developed spontaneous tumours later. 22.9% of rapamycin-treated mice were still alive when the last control mouse died. The paper provided evidence that an intermittent rapamycin schedule can extend lifespan in a normal inbred mouse strain, adding to earlier results in genetically heterogeneous mice. Boundary: Female mice of a single inbred strain (129/Sv) only; drafted from the abstract only, so dose, group sizes and median-lifespan statistics are not given here.

data.title: The TSC1-2 tumor suppressor controls insulin-PI3K signaling via regulation of IRS proteins
data.authors: Harrington LS; Findlay GM; Gray A; Tolkacheva T; Wigfield S; Rebholz H; Barnett J; Leslie NR; Cheng S; Shepherd PR; Gout I; Downes CP; Lamb RF

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: One of two 2004 papers that placed mTORC1's main negative feedback loop downstream of TSC-Rheb-S6K1 (rapamycin-sensitive IRS-1 degradation had been reported earlier, Haruta 2000). When mTORC1/S6K1 activity is left switched on, S6K1 phosphorylates IRS-1 and represses its expression, so the insulin receptor can no longer signal to PI3K. This is the textbook explanation for why blocking mTORC1 paradoxically raises Akt activity, and it contributes to insulin resistance when mTORC1 is chronically overactive (for example with TSC loss or nutrient excess). The insulin resistance seen with chronic rapamycin is instead attributed mainly to mTORC2 disruption (LAM2012).

data.title: mTOR inhibition improves immune function in the elderly
data.authors: Mannick JB; Del Giudice G; Lattanzi M; Valiante NM; Praestgaard J; Huang B; Lonetto MA; Maecker HT; Kovarik J; Carson S; Glass DJ; Klickstein LB

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

The share of T cells carrying the exhaustion marker PD-1 also fell. The PEARL authors summarise the doses as 0.5 mg daily or 5 mg weekly for 6 weeks. This is the human result behind the weekly low-dose idea. Boundary: a stronger vaccine response is a lab marker, not fewer infections, and the later RTB101 trial (MAN2021) shows how that gap can matter.

data.finding: Conditional deletion of Rictor in the postnatal mouse forebrain reduced mTORC2 activity and selectively impaired long-term memory and the late phase of hippocampal LTP, with a comparable long-term-memory deficit in dTORC2-deficient flies. Hippocampal actin polymerisation was reduced, and restoring it rescued both L-LTP and long-term memory; a compound that raised mTORC2 activity converted early LTP into late LTP and enhanced memory. This is the loss-of-function AND rescue evidence that mTORC2 is required for memory consolidation - the arm chronic rapamycin also disrupts, and the study Open Question H8 needs for its mTORC2 liability leg, which until 2026-09-05 rested on no supporting study at all.

data.authors: Wang J; Ni Z; Zhang Xinxin; He L; Cheng X; Huang L; Ye H; Li P; Zhao TJ; Du X
data.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

Loss of the core subunits VPS18 or VPS11 starves the cell of amino acids, switches on the integrated stress response and shuts down mTORC1; enforced mTORC1 activity rescues the proliferative defect while BIM deletion rescues survival, separating the two failure modes. data.title: Hepatic mTORC2 activates glycolysis and lipogenesis through Akt, glucokinase, and SREBP1c
data.authors: Hagiwara A; Cornu M; Cybulski N; Polak P; Betz C; Trapani F; Terracciano L; Heim MH; Rüegg MA; Hall MN

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Liver-specific rictor knockout mice (LiRiKO); primary hepatocytes with constitutively active Akt2 or glucokinase rescue
data.finding: The authors deleted rictor, an essential mTORC2 component, only in mouse liver. In fed knockout mice the liver lost Akt Ser473 phosphorylation and had lower glucokinase and SREBP1c activity, so it kept making glucose (gluconeogenesis) while glycolysis and fat synthesis fell, as if it could not sense that the animal had eaten. The mice became hyperglycaemic and hyperinsulinaemic with low blood lipids. In mTORC2-deficient hepatocytes, constitutively active Akt2 restored both glucose flux and lipogenesis, while extra glucokinase restored glucose flux but not lipogenesis, placing Akt as the main route from hepatic mTORC2 to these outputs. Boundary: Mouse liver with lifelong genetic loss of mTORC2, plus cultured mouse hepatocytes. Not a drug study and not tested in people. Drafted from the abstract only.

data.title: Randomized phase II study of multiple dose levels of CCI-779, a novel mammalian target of rapamycin kinase inhibitor, in patients with advanced refractory renal cell carcinoma
data.authors: Atkins MB; Hidalgo M; Stadler WM; Logan TF; Dutcher JP; Hudes GR; Park Y; Liou SH; Marshall B; Boni JP; Dukart G; Sherman ML

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Humans: 111 patients with advanced refractory renal cell carcinoma, randomised to three weekly IV doses of temsirolimus (CCI-779)
data.finding: In this randomised phase II trial, 111 patients with advanced renal cell carcinoma that had progressed on earlier therapy received temsirolimus (CCI-779) at 25, 75 or 250 mg as a weekly intravenous infusion. There was no control arm: randomisation compared dose levels only. The objective response rate was 7% (1 complete and 7 partial responses), with minor responses in a further 26%; median time to progression was 5.8 months and median survival 15.0 months. Neither efficacy nor toxicity differed significantly between the three doses, which supported taking the lowest dose (25 mg) forward. The commonest side effects were rash (76%), mouth sores (70%), weakness (50%) and nausea (43%); the commonest grade 3-4 events were high blood glucose (17%), low phosphate (13%), anaemia (9%) and high triglycerides (6%). Boundary: patients with advanced, previously treated kidney cancer; no placebo or active comparator, so survival figures cannot be attributed to the drug; risk-group analysis was retrospective.

data.title: siRNA screening of the kinome identifies ULK1 as a multidomain modulator of autophagy
data.authors: Chan EY; Kir S; Tooze SA

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: HEK293 cells (GFP-LC3 lipidation assay, kinome siRNA library); HeLa cells; rat ULK1 constructs
data.finding: The authors screened a kinase-targeted siRNA library in human HEK293 cells, using lipidation of the autophagy marker GFP-LC3 after amino-acid starvation as the readout. ULK1 came out of the screen: knocking it down blocked starvation-induced autophagy, while knocking down the related kinase ULK2 did not. ULK1 knockdown also blocked autophagy induced by rapamycin, which fits ULK1 acting downstream of mTOR. Overexpressed ULK1 inhibited autophagy independently of its kinase activity, and the dominant-negative effect mapped to residues 1-351, while the conserved C-terminal domain was needed for ULK1 to reach cytoplasmic structures, some of them LC3-positive. One of the early papers to place ULK1 as a required kinase for starvation-induced autophagy in mammalian cells. Boundary: Cultured human cell lines with siRNA and overexpression; no whole-animal data. The link to mTOR rests on rapamycin-induced autophagy, not on a measurement of mTORC1 acting on ULK1. Drafted from the abstract only (no PMC full text).

data.title: Prolonged rapamycin treatment inhibits mTORC2 assembly and Akt/PKB
data.authors: Sarbassov DD; Ali SM; Sengupta S; Sheen JH; Hsu PP; Bagley AF; Markhard AL; Sabatini DM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: The molecular explanation for rapamycin's dark side. Short-term rapamycin only hits mTORC1, but prolonged treatment can also inhibit the assembly of NEW mTORC2 in susceptible cell types, reducing mTORC2 abundance and cutting Akt signaling over time. The wording matters: this is prevention of new assembly, not the dismantling of complexes already built, and the response depends on cell context and length of exposure. This is the mechanistic root of the insulin-resistance side effect later shown in mice (see Lamming 2012) - crucial for anyone dosing rapamycin for longevity.

Suppressing mTORC2 — but not mTORC1 — returns the accelerated microtubule polymerisation and neuronal hypertrophy of Pten-KO neurons to wild-type levels, and the effect is confined to the axonal growth cone rather than the proximal axon shaft. A clean genetic dissection on the comparatively thin mTORC2 side of the pathway.

data.title: The metabolic checkpoint kinase mTOR is essential for IL-15 signaling during the development and activation of NK cells
data.authors: Marcais A; Cherfils-Vicini J; Viant C; Degouve S; Viel S; Fenis A; Rabilloud J; Mayol K; Tavares A; Bienvenu J; Gangloff YG; Gilson E; Vivier E; Walzer T

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: NKp46-cre x Mtor-flox mice (NK-cell-specific mTOR deletion) plus acute TAT-Cre deletion and adoptive transfer; poly(I:C) and MCMV or influenza infection; oral rapamycin (sirolimus, 100 ug/day) with an in vivo missing-self rejection assay; Seahorse metabolic profiling; human NK cells from healthy donors stimulated with IL-2 plus rapamycin, PP242 or Ku-0063794
data.finding: This study separated two arms of IL-15 signalling in NK cells by dose: low IL-15 mainly phosphorylated STAT5 (EC50 about 1.5 ng/ml), while higher IL-15 was needed to switch on mTOR (EC50 about 5.3 ng/ml for S6 phosphorylation), and IL-15 was the only one of many tested stimuli that strongly raised pS6. Deleting mTOR in NK cells left bone-marrow numbers normal but blocked the CD11b-low to double-positive transition, cut proliferation about three-fold and left almost no mature NK cells in the periphery, with lower CD71, glucose uptake and about half the surface CD122 and CD132, so the receptor feedback is itself mTOR-dependent. In activation, mTOR-deficient NK cells failed to grow or raise nutrient uptake after poly(I:C) and made about half as much granzyme B, while IFN-gamma production in response to IL-12 plus IL-18 stayed normal. Oral rapamycin lowered pS6 and granzyme B in vivo and made rejection of MHC-class-I-negative target cells significantly less efficient, and mTOR inhibitors also blocked IL-2-driven granzyme B induction in human NK cells. Boundary: mouse genetics and mouse in vivo pharmacology, with the human arm limited to healthy-donor NK cells stimulated in culture; the clinical implication for patients on rapalogs is inference, not a measured patient outcome.

data.authors: List EO; Berryman DE; Lach GS; Minto DF; Weese K; Kopchick JJ

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: GHA transgenic mice expressing the bovine GH G119K receptor antagonist (line maintained since 1991), both sexes; independent 2-year-old frailty cohort
data.finding: Transgenic expression of a growth hormone receptor antagonist — the G119K mutant chemistry behind the FDA-approved drug Pegvisomant — significantly extended both median and maximal lifespan in male (p = 0.044; p = 0.0037) and female mice, with maximal lifespan extended by 186 and 265 days respectively. Two-year-old antagonist mice were less frail and had greater grip strength despite increased adiposity. data.title: Targeting the biology of ageing with mTOR inhibitors to improve immune function in older adults: phase 2b and phase 3 randomised trials
data.authors: Mannick JB; Teo G; Bernardo P; Quinn D; Russell K; Klickstein L; Marshall W; Shergill S

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: This paper reports two trials of RTB101, a drug that blocks mTOR, taken once a day for 16 weeks by adults over 65. In the phase 2b trial (652 people), fewer people on 10 mg had a lab-confirmed respiratory infection than on placebo (19% against 28%), but that result comes from a pooled analysis the authors did not correct for multiple testing, and the corrected analysis did not reach significance. The phase 3 trial (1,024 people) used a different main endpoint, set with the FDA: symptoms with or without a lab test. It found no difference (26% against 25%, p = 0.65), although blood tests still showed more antiviral genes switched on in both trials. In phase 2b, twice-daily dosing and a combination with everolimus did not reach significance, which the authors read as a hint that on-off inhibition may beat constant inhibition. Those numbers are "data not shown" in the paper. Boundary: RTB101 is not rapamycin or everolimus, the phase 3 group was healthier (no COPD, no smokers), and that trial was too small to test the lab-confirmed endpoint. The only everolimus arm (RTB101 plus everolimus 0.1 mg daily) was a combination and did not reach significance, which is why this paper is listed against the everolimus and immune function link on the pathway map. It cannot show what everolimus alone does.

data.title: Excitatory/inhibitory synaptic imbalance leads to hippocampal hyperexcitability in mouse models of tuberous sclerosis
data.authors: Bateup HS; Johnson CA; Denefrio CL; Saulnier JL; Kornacker K; Sabatini BL

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Tsc1 floxed mice: lentiviral Cre in dissociated hippocampal cultures (multi-electrode arrays, microarrays); CaMKIIa-Cre forebrain cKO (kainate seizures); sparse or widespread AAV-Cre in CA1 with slice electrophysiology; rapamycin in vitro and in vivo
data.finding: Deleting Tsc1 from cultured mouse hippocampal neurons raised phospho-S6 and made the network fire more than twice as much as controls by day 14, in an epilepsy-like bursting pattern; four days of rapamycin brought activity back to control levels. Many gene-expression and synaptic changes in the knockout cultures, such as high Arc and fewer surface AMPA receptors, turned out to be secondary responses to the high activity, not direct effects of mTOR. In hippocampal CA1, Tsc1 loss in single pyramidal neurons weakened the inhibitory synaptic input they received and raised their excitation/inhibition ratio, while their intrinsic excitability was lower, not higher. Forebrain Tsc1 knockout mice had more severe kainate-induced seizures (80% died, while all controls survived), and seven days of rapamycin in vivo restored inhibition and normalised the E/I ratio. Boundary: mouse neurons, cultures and brain slices; Tsc1 deleted in excitatory neurons only; seizure test used a chemical convulsant.

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure

Blocking mTOR with rapamycin in hippocampal slices reduced late-phase long-term potentiation (LTP) after high-frequency stimulation, while early-phase LTP was unaffected. Rapamycin also blocked the synaptic potentiation induced by the growth factor BDNF. This was one of the early papers to tie a rapamycin-sensitive pathway to the protein-synthesis-dependent phase of synaptic plasticity and to suggest it controls local translation at synapses. Boundary: rodent brain slices and cultured neurons; mTOR targets were localised but their phosphorylation during LTP was not reported in the abstract; no behaviour or memory test.

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: The authors systematically tested whether lowering protein synthesis extends lifespan in the worm C. elegans. Reducing ribosomal proteins, the S6 kinase homologue rsks-1 or translation-initiation factors increased lifespan, and these perturbations, like TOR inhibition, increased resistance to heat stress. Different kinds of translation inhibition split into two groups: one that needed the FOXO transcription factor DAF-16 for the lifespan and stress effects and one that did not. The results linked TOR, but not sir-2.1, to the lifespan extension caused by dietary restriction in worms, and suggested that neither TOR inhibition nor dietary restriction works simply by reducing total protein synthesis. data.title: Structural basis for mTORC1 activation on the lysosomal membrane
data.authors: Cui Z; Esposito A; Napolitano G; Ballabio A; Hurley JH

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Cryo-EM structure (human proteins, reconstituted on membranes) + validation in inducible RAPTOR-KO MEFs
data.finding: Resolves how mTORC1 flips from 'parked on the lysosome' to 'catalytically switched on'. Reconstituting the whole assembly on membranes from purified Rheb, Rag GTPases, Ragulator and mTORC1, cryo-EM shows the kinase reaches full activity only after two separate anchoring steps: Rag-Ragulator first pulls it to within about 100 angstroms of the membrane, then Rheb pulls it to within about 40 angstroms, and only when Raptor and mTOR itself also touch the membrane directly do the catalytic residues line up for full activity. Growth-factor input (via Rheb) and nutrient input (via the Rags) are shown converging on the same physical docking event rather than acting through separate switches. Boundary: reconstituted on synthetic membranes from purified components — a structural/biochemical model, not a measurement inside a living cell.

data.title: Sterol regulatory element-binding proteins are essential for the metabolic programming of effector T cells and adaptive immunity
data.authors: Kidani Y; Elsaesser H; Hock MB; Vergnes L; Williams KJ; Argus JP; Marbois BN; Komisopoulou E; Wilson EB; Osborne TF; Graeber TG; Reue K; Brooks DG; Bensinger SJ

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Mouse T cells with Cd4-cre-driven deletion of Scap (removing both SREBP1 and SREBP2 activity), siRNA and constitutively active SREBP constructs, rapamycin and LY294002 pretreatment, ChIP for SREBP1/2 at lipogenic promoters, GC-MS lipid measurement, Seahorse profiling, LCMV-Armstrong infection and homeostatic-proliferation transfers
data.finding: Activating T cells switch on cholesterol and fatty acid synthesis genes within hours, and this paper showed the switch runs through PI3K and mTOR to SREBP: 100 nM rapamycin given 30 minutes before stimulation blocked the induction of the lipogenic programme, prevented processing of full-length SREBP and its accumulation in the nucleus, and reduced SREBP1 and SREBP2 occupancy at lipogenic promoters to background. Deleting Scap in T cells, which removes both SREBP1 and SREBP2 activity, left thymic and peripheral T-cell numbers normal but the cells could not blast: they entered G1 and stalled, failed to raise cholesterol and fatty acids after activation, and increased ECAR and OCR only modestly where controls rose about ten-fold and four-fold. Adding cholesterol conjugated to methyl-beta-cyclodextrin roughly doubled survival at 48 hours (21 to 45 percent) and restored growth, cell-cycle entry and ER expansion, which points to cholesterol as the limiting step. After LCMV-Armstrong infection the Scap-deficient mice had fewer virus-specific CD8 T cells with lower IFN-gamma and TNF, while homeostatic proliferation was unaffected. Boundary: mouse genetics and mouse cells; the mTOR step is shown with rapamycin pretreatment in cultured T cells, and the in vivo arm measures the consequence of losing SREBP activity rather than of inhibiting mTOR.

data.model_system: Human and hamster cell lines (HeLa, CHO)
data.finding: Opens a second, non-canonical route by which amino acids reach mTORC1. The class III PI 3-kinase hVps34 is switched off by amino acid or glucose starvation and by AMPK activation, and is required for S6K1 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation, yet it sits outside the insulin/class I PI3K input (it does not affect Akt or TSC2 phosphorylation). Boundary: cell lines and knockdown/overexpression only; the step is nutrient-regulated but the sensor itself is not identified.

data.title: LncRNA DLX6-AS1 promotes necroptosis through PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway in myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury mice
data.authors: Su Y; Mu L; Wang L; Li T; Zhang Q; Zhang Jun

evidence.label: Animal model

data.finding: LncRNA DLX6-AS1 activates PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling to promote necroptosis in myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury; inhibiting DLX6-AS1 suppresses necroptosis and protects cardiomyocytes.

data.title: Mutations in DEPDC5 cause familial focal epilepsy with variable foci
data.authors: Dibbens LM; de Vries B; Donatello S; Heron SE; Hodgson BL; Chintawar S; Crompton DE; Hughes JN; Bellows ST; Klein KM; Callenbach PM; Corbett MA; Gardner AE; Kivity S; Iona X; Regan BM; Weller CM; Crimmins D; O'Brien TJ; Guerrero-López R; Mulley JC; Dubeau F; Licchetta L; Bisulli F; Cossette P; Thomas PQ; Gecz J; Serratosa J; Brouwer OF; Andermann F; Andermann E; van den Maagdenberg AM; Pandolfo M; Berkovic SF; Scheffer IE

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Humans; families with focal epilepsy (exome sequencing + linkage; 10/82 families)
data.finding: Exome sequencing and linkage in families with autosomal dominant familial focal epilepsy with variable foci identified loss-of-function mutations in DEPDC5, a GATOR1 subunit, in 5 of 6 additional published large families and in roughly 12% (10/82) of smaller focal-epilepsy families. This is the human genetic anchor for GATOR1's physiological importance: it supports that loss of a GATOR1 subunit produces a human phenotype. Observational genetic association within families, not an interventional study, and the paper carries no mTORC1 readout of its own - the link to the pathway rests on the molecular work (BAR2013, SHE2018), not on this study.

data.title: Raptor, a binding partner of target of rapamycin (TOR), mediates TOR action
data.authors: Hara K; Maruki Y; Long X; Yoshino K; Oshiro N; Hidayat S; Tokunaga C; Avruch J; Yonezawa K

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Independent co-discovery of Raptor (same issue of Cell as Kim 2002). Showed Raptor is essential for mTOR to phosphorylate 4E-BP1 and S6K1, and that knocking it down in worms mimics loss of TOR - confirming Raptor as a core, conserved mediator of TOR action.

data.title: Structure of mammalian AMPK and its regulation by ADP
data.authors: Xiao B; Sanders MJ; Underwood E; Heath R; Mayer FV; Carmena D; Jing C; Walker PA; Eccleston JF; Haire LF; Saiu P; Howell SA; Aasland R; Martin SR; Carling D; Gamblin SJ

data.finding: AMP binding to the gamma regulatory domain promotes phosphorylation of AMPK and protects it from dephosphorylation. ADP binding to one site also protects against dephosphorylation but does not activate allosterically. Crystal structure of an active AMPK complex.

data.title: Enhanced sensitivity of PTEN-deficient tumors to inhibition of FRAP/mTOR
data.authors: Neshat MS; Mellinghoff IK; Tran C; Stiles B; Thomas G; Petersen R; Frost P; Gibbons JJ; Wu H; Sawyers CL

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Isogenic PTEN+/+ and PTEN-/- mouse cells and human cancer cell lines, in vitro and as tumours in mice; CCI-779
data.finding: Tested whether tumour cells that have lost PTEN depend more on mTOR. The rapamycin analogue CCI-779 (temsirolimus) blocked growth of PTEN-null cells and tumours preferentially, and reversed the extra tumour growth caused by constitutively active Akt, placing mTOR downstream of Akt in tumour formation. PTEN loss went with higher S6 kinase activity and S6 phosphorylation. Sensitivity was not explained by how well the drug blocked S6 phosphorylation, since S6 was inhibited in sensitive and resistant lines alike. Boundary: worked from the abstract only (scanned PMC record); mouse and human cell lines and mouse tumour models, not patients.

data.title: An inhibitor of mTOR reduces neoplasia and normalizes p70/S6 kinase activity in Pten+/- mice
data.authors: Podsypanina K; Lee RT; Politis C; Hennessy I; Crane A; Puc J; Neshat M; Wang H; Yang L; Gibbons J; Frost P; Dreisbach V; Blenis J; Gaciong Z; Fisher P; Sawyers CL; Hedrick-Ellenson L; Parsons R

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Pten+/- mice treated with a pharmacological mTOR inhibitor
data.finding: Transformed cells in Pten+/- mice showed raised phosphorylated Akt and active p70 S6 kinase together with faster proliferation. Treating the mice with an mTOR inhibitor reduced neoplastic proliferation, tumour size and S6 kinase activity without changing Akt status. The authors concluded that S6K and possibly other mTOR targets contribute to tumour development downstream of PTEN loss. Boundary: worked from the abstract only (scanned PMC record); mouse model. The abstract does not name the inhibitor.

data.title: mTOR kinase inhibition causes feedback-dependent biphasic regulation of AKT signaling
data.authors: Rodrik-Outmezguine VS; Chandarlapaty S; Pagano NC; Poulikakos PI; Scaltriti M; Moskatel E; Baselga J; Guichard S; Rosen N

data.title: mTOR inhibition augments antitumor immune effector response by reprogramming the TP53-mutant, immune-cold HNSCC tumor microenvironment
data.authors: Nath P; Khandelwal A; Li C; Moore-Medlin T; Vasudevan SS; Alvarez VA; Franco OE; Gutkind JS; Nathan CO

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Syngeneic mouse models of TP53-mutant HNSCC
data.finding: In syngeneic TP53-mutant HNSCC mouse models, the mTOR inhibitor everolimus reprogrammed the immune-cold tumor microenvironment: it increased CD8+ T cell and dendritic cell infiltration, reduced Tregs and HIF-1α/VEGFA-driven MDSC recruitment, boosted TNF-α/CXCL10 chemokine signaling, and reduced PD-1/PD-L1 expression — restoring T-cell cytotoxic competence and suppressing tumor growth.

data.title: Spatial coupling of mTOR and autophagy augments secretory phenotypes
data.authors: Narita Masako; Young AR; Arakawa S; Samarajiwa SA; Nakashima T; Yoshida S; Hong S; Berry LS; Reichelt S; Ferreira M; Tavare S; Inoki K; Shimizu S; Narita Masashi

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human and mouse cells (Ras-induced senescent fibroblasts, macrophages, podocytes)
data.finding: Protein synthesis and autophagic degradation are usually described as opposites that mTOR switches between, and this paper shows a compartment where the cell deliberately runs both at once. In senescent cells, autolysosomes and mTOR gather at one side of the Golgi (the TASCC), mTOR gets there in an amino-acid- and Rag-dependent way, and destroying that arrangement cuts interleukin-6/8 secretion. Boundary: cells, not organisms; it explains how the senescent secretory programme is fuelled, not whether blocking it helps an animal.

data.title: mTORC1 Couples Nucleotide Synthesis to Nucleotide Demand Resulting in a Targetable Metabolic Vulnerability
data.authors: Valvezan AJ; Turner M; Belaid A; Lam HC; Miller SK; McNamara MC; Baglini C; Housden BE; Perrimon N; Kwiatkowski DJ; Asara JM; Henske EP; Manning BD

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Hyperactive mTORC1 couples nucleotide synthesis to demand; imbalance drives replication stress in these cells.

data.title: G3BPs tether the TSC complex to lysosomes and suppress mTORC1 signaling
data.authors: Prentzell MT; Rehbein U; Cadena Sandoval M; De Meulemeester AS; Baumeister R; Brohée L; Berdel B; Bockwoldt M; Carroll B; Chowdhury SR; von Deimling A; Demetriades C; Figlia G; de Araujo MEG; Heberle AM; Heiland I; Holzwarth B; Huber LA; Jaworski J; Kedra M; Kern K; Kopach A; Korolchuk VI; van 't Land-Kuper I; Macias M; Nellist M; Palm W; Pusch S; Ramos Pittol JM; Reil M; Reintjes A; Reuter F; Sampson JR; Scheldeman C; Siekierska A; Stefan E; Teleman AA; Thomas LE; Torres-Quesada O; Trump S; West HD; de Witte P; Woltering S; Yordanov TE; Zmorzynska J; Opitz CA; Thedieck K

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human and mouse cells; breast cancer patient data; zebrafish
data.finding: Adds a physical brake upstream of mTORC1. G3BP1 and G3BP2, known until then as core stress-granule proteins, also sit on the cytoplasmic face of the lysosome and are what holds the TSC complex there; without them TSC cannot reach its target and mTORC1 becomes over-responsive to amino acids and insulin. Loss of G3BP1 reproduces TSC-like hyperactivity phenotypes: faster mTORC1-driven motility in breast cancer cells, with low G3BP1 correlating with worse patient outcome, and disturbed neuronal development in zebrafish. Relevant to the Atlas because it is a lysosomal tethering step that the canonical Rheb/TSC diagram does not show.

data.title: A role for autophagy in the extension of lifespan by dietary restriction in C. elegans
data.authors: Hansen M; Chandra A; Mitic LL; Onken B; Driscoll M; Kenyon C

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Makes autophagy a necessary step between dietary restriction and a longer life, not a side effect of it: blocking autophagy genes abolishes the lifespan extension produced both by dietary restriction and by TOR inhibition. The paper is equally careful about what autophagy cannot do on its own, because autophagy still runs in animals lacking DAF-16/FOXO and yet those animals are not long-lived. Boundary: worms; necessity was shown, sufficiency was not.

data.title: High Responsiveness of Head and Neck Kaposiform Hemangioendothelioma Without Kasabach-Merritt Phenomenon to Sirolimus Monotherapy.
data.authors: Xu Y; Zhou J; Lan Y; Yang L; Zhang Y; Ji Y

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: In 71 children with kaposiform haemangioendothelioma without Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, head and neck lesions achieved a 100% 12-month radiologic response to sirolimus monotherapy versus 76% elsewhere; anatomical location was the only independent predictor of response. Observational: a matched multicentre cohort, not a randomised comparison, so confounding by indication and by lesion characteristics cannot be excluded and the association between site and response is not established as causal.

data.title: Translational control of long-lasting synaptic plasticity and memory
data.authors: Costa-Mattioli M; Sossin WS; Klann E; Sonenberg N

evidence.label: Review — secondary literature, not a new result
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Narrative review (no new data): genetic, physiological, pharmacological and biochemical studies in rodents, Aplysia and Drosophila
data.finding: This review gathers evidence that long-lasting synaptic plasticity and long-term memory depend on new protein synthesis, and that the step where mRNA translation starts is a main control point. It covers two arms: the mTORC1 arm (4E-BP2, eIF4E, S6K) that controls cap-dependent translation, and the eIF2alpha arm (GCN2, PKR, ATF4) that controls general translation and specific mRNAs. It also discusses how faulty translational control is linked to disorders such as fragile X syndrome and tuberous sclerosis. It is a summary of work by many labs and gives the field a shared framework rather than new data. Boundary: narrative review; the cited evidence is mainly from rodent slices, rodent behaviour and invertebrate models, not from people.

data.title: Rapamycin Attenuates Age-Related Changes in Marmoset Submandibular Gland: A Non-Human Primate Model of Human Oral Aging.
data.authors: Abdul-Azees PA; Wang H; Chen J; Marinkovic M; Dean DD; Chen XD; Salmon AB; Yeh CK

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), chronic oral rapamycin, submandibular gland histology and immunofluorescence
data.finding: In the aging marmoset submandibular gland the authors found fewer mucous and serous acinar units, expansion of ductal and collagen-rich stromal compartments, more extracellular matrix remodeling, dysregulated lipid metabolism, and more apoptotic and senescent cells. Chronic oral rapamycin was associated with partial preservation of acinar structure and with less fibrosis, lipid accumulation and fewer apoptotic and senescent cells, giving a tissue picture closer to that of younger animals. Boundary: histological and immunofluorescence associations in one tissue of a short-lived primate; the abstract gives no dose or group sizes, does not show that gland function improved, and reports no lifespan outcome.

data.title: Aging preserves mTORC1 but attenuates JNK-SMAD2L signaling sensitivity to passive stretch-induced tension development in isolated mouse skeletal muscle.
data.authors: Kristiansen JB; Andresen J; Jakobsgaard JE; Vissing K

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Mouse (ex vivo EDL muscle, adult 16-week vs old 24-month female mice)
data.finding: Passive mechanical stretch activated mTORC1 signalling (mTOR, p70S6K, rpS6, 4E-BP1) to a similar degree in ex vivo muscle from adult and old female mice, whereas JNK-SMAD2L activation by the same stretch was blunted with age, suggesting mTORC1 mechanosensitivity itself is preserved in this model.

data.title: The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin: The Grand ConducTOR of Metabolism and Aging
data.authors: Kennedy BK; Lamming DW

evidence.label: Review — secondary literature, not a new result
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: A Cell Metabolism review framing mTOR as the 'grand conductor' that coordinates whole-body metabolism, tissue by tissue. Especially valuable for its clear-eyed section on WHY rapamycin causes metabolic side effects (the mTORC2 problem) - which is the main barrier to using it against aging. Pairs perfectly with Lamming's own 2012 mechanism paper.

data.title: Chronic inhibition of mammalian target of rapamycin by rapamycin modulates cognitive and non-cognitive components of behavior throughout lifespan in mice.
data.authors: Halloran J; Hussong SA; Burbank R; Podlutskaya N; Fischer KE; Sloane LB; Austad SN; Strong R; Richardson A; Hart MJ; Galvan V

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Asked whether the lifespan-extending dose of rapamycin harms or helps the aging BRAIN. Reassuringly, it enhanced learning and memory in young mice, prevented age-related cognitive decline in old ones, and even reduced anxiety and depression-like behavior - linked to boosted brain monoamines. Cognitive benefit, not cost.

data.title: mTOR signaling in growth control and disease
data.authors: Laplante M; Sabatini DM

evidence.label: Review — secondary literature, not a new result
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: The classic 2012 Cell review that became the standard reference for mTOR signaling. Comprehensive yet readable synthesis of how mTOR integrates environmental cues to control growth, and how its deregulation drives cancer, obesity, diabetes and neurodegeneration. A perfect companion to the newer 2020 review.

data.title: mTORC1-TFEB/TFE3 signaling is associated with bile acid diversification during hepatic metabolic adaptation
data.authors: Zaufel A; Sun W; Pastore N; Taschler U; Wagner C; Hackl H; Sommer J; Silbert-Wagner D; Hengstler JG; Begher-Tibbe B; Stauber R; Kolb D; Troetzmueller M; Gottschalk B; Thorsheim C; Stange EL; Hornef MW; Pivovarova-Ramich O; Pfeiffer AFH; Matchett KP; Loft A; Herzig S; Henderson NC; Ballabio A; Arany Z; Wolfrum C; Fickert P; Moustafa T

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Mouse (liver-specific genetic mTORC1/TFEB manipulation, rapamycin treatment, dietary protein restriction); correlative human MASLD patient cohort
data.finding: Establishes a new mTORC1-TFEB/TFE3 signaling axis controlling hepatic bile acid metabolism. Depending on mTORC1 signaling state, mice show coordinated shifts in bile-acid species (non-12-OH vs 12-OH) via altered enzyme expression and cholesterol trafficking; these shifts are reversed by mTORC1 pathway deletion or rapamycin treatment. Dietary protein restriction (which inhibits mTORC1) produces a similar bile-acid shift in mice and correlates with improved metabolic outcomes in human MASLD patients, linking mTORC1 nutrient sensing directly to bile-acid homeostasis and fatty liver disease.

data.title: A bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitor overcomes drug resistance in breast cancer
data.authors: Meng D; Zhao X; Yang YC; Navickas A; Helland C; Goodarzi H; Singh M; Bandyopadhyay S

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human ER+/HER2- breast cancer cell lines; mouse patient-derived xenografts (PDX)
data.finding: RMC-6272, a bi-steric molecule with >25-fold selectivity for mTORC1 over mTORC2, completely suppresses mTORC1 (hitting the rapamycin-resistant substrate 4E-BP1) and overcomes hormone- and CDK4/6-inhibitor resistance in breast cancer cell lines and PDX -- the preclinical basis for the RMC-5552 selective-inhibitor clinical program.

data.title: DNA methylation age analysis of rapamycin in common marmosets.
data.authors: Horvath S; Zoller JA; Haghani A; Lu AT; Raj K; Jasinska AJ; Mattison JA; Salmon AB

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus) whole blood, DNA methylation array, rapamycin cohort; vervet and rhesus macaque for clock comparison
data.finding: The authors built two epigenetic clocks for common marmoset blood from DNA methylation data; the human-marmoset clock for relative age correlated moderately well with age in vervet monkeys and rhesus macaques. In a separate marmoset cohort they tested whether rapamycin would change epigenetic age. The clocks did not detect a significant effect of rapamycin on the epigenetic age of marmoset blood. Boundary: a null result on one biomarker (DNA methylation age in blood). It does not show that rapamycin has no effect on aging in marmosets, only that these clocks did not register one; the abstract gives no dose, duration or group size.

data.title: In Vivo Decoding Mechanisms of the Temporal Patterns of Blood Insulin by the Insulin-AKT Pathway in the Liver
data.authors: Kubota H; Uda S; Matsuzaki F; Yamauchi Y; Kuroda S

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Rat liver in vivo (hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp with different insulin time patterns) plus mathematical model
data.finding: The in-vivo follow-up to KUB2012. In rat liver, all temporal patterns of blood insulin were encoded at the insulin receptor, and downstream molecules decoded them selectively through AKT: S6K read the additional (pulse-like) secretion, G6Pase the basal secretion via FoxO1, GSK3-beta all of it. Modelling tied the selectivity to network structure, sensitivity and time constants. Shows that pattern decoding is not only a cell-culture effect.

data.title: Adipose-specific knockout of raptor results in lean mice with enhanced mitochondrial respiration
data.authors: Polak P; Cybulski N; Feige JN; Auwerx J; Rüegg MA; Hall MN

evidence.label: Animal model

data.finding: Adipose raptor knockout yields lean, metabolically protected mice, revealing mTORC1's role in fat metabolism.

data.authors: Kim E; Goraksha-Hicks P; Li L; Neufeld TP; Guan KL

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure

data.finding: Rag GTPases mediate amino-acid signalling to TORC1 (parallel discovery to Sancak 2008).

data.title: Ablation in mice of the mTORC components raptor, rictor, or mLST8 reveals that mTORC2 is required for signaling to Akt-FOXO and PKCalpha, but not S6K1
data.authors: Guertin DA; Stevens DM; Thoreen CC; Burds AA; Kalaany NY; Moffat J; Brown M; Fitzgerald KJ; Sabatini DM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: The foundational genetic 'dissection' of the two complexes in living mice. Deleting Raptor was lethal early (mTORC1 essential); deleting Rictor or mLST8 selectively knocked out mTORC2 signaling to Akt and PKCalpha but spared S6K1. This cleanly assigned jobs to each complex and showed mLST8 is an mTORC2-specific requirement in mice.

data.title: Genetic and biochemical characterization of dTOR, the Drosophila homolog of the target of rapamycin
data.authors: Oldham S; Montagne J; Radimerski T; Thomas G; Hafen E

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Drosophila melanogaster dTOR mutants (partial and full loss), genetic interaction with insulin pathway; biochemistry of dS6K
data.finding: The authors identified and characterised dTOR, the fruit fly version of TOR. Genetic and biochemical experiments indicated that dTOR affects growth in a cell-autonomous way by changing the activity of the fly S6 kinase, dS6K, and so connects to the insulin signalling pathway. Unlike other insulin pathway components, partial loss of dTOR reduced growth mainly in endoreplicating tissues, which copy their DNA without dividing. The authors read this as evidence that dTOR sits on a parallel pathway that senses amino acids. Boundary: Drosophila genetics and biochemistry; the parallel amino acid pathway is an interpretation from fly phenotypes, not a direct measurement of amino acid sensing.

data.title: Cutting edge: distinct glycolytic and lipid oxidative metabolic programs are essential for effector and regulatory CD4+ T cell subsets
data.authors: Michalek RD; Gerriets VA; Jacobs SR; Macintyre AN; MacIver NJ; Mason EF; Sullivan SA; Nichols AG; Rathmell JC

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Primary mouse CD4 T cells polarised in vitro to Th1, Th2, Th17 and inducible Treg, with rapamycin, metformin or the CPT1 inhibitor etomoxir; Glut1-transgenic and Glut1-myc knock-in mice; OVA-driven allergic asthma model with metformin
data.finding: Comparing CD4 T cells grown under effector and regulatory conditions, the authors showed that Th1, Th2 and Th17 cells carry high surface Glut1 and are strongly glycolytic, while inducible Treg carry little Glut1, oxidise lipid at a higher rate and have more phosphorylated AMPK. Blocking lipid oxidation with etomoxir selectively suppressed Treg generation and left effector differentiation intact, whereas removing glucose blocked Th17 but not Treg. Both rapamycin and metformin raised fatty acid oxidation in stimulated CD4 T cells, and etomoxir prevented the Treg increase produced by rapamycin or TGF-beta, which ties the pro-Treg effect of mTOR inhibition to lipid oxidation. In a mouse asthma model, metformin lowered Glut1 on activated CD4 T cells and increased the proportion and number of Treg in draining lymph nodes, although airway responsiveness itself did not change significantly. Boundary: mouse cells and one mouse allergic-airway model; mTOR inhibition is pharmacological (rapamycin) and mTOR activity was not measured directly, so the mTOR arm is inferred from drug effects.

data.title: Carvedilol attenuates PTZ-induced epileptogenesis: associations with hippocampal neuroinflammation and PI3K/AKT/mTOR-related alterations.
data.authors: Madkour AH; Abdelaziz RR; Nader MA; Elshal M

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Prophylactic carvedilol reduced seizure scores, hippocampal damage and NLRP3-driven neuroinflammation in PTZ-kindled rats, with accompanying changes in PI3K/AKT/mTOR-related protein expression; the authors explicitly state causality was not established.

data.title: An ANGPTL8-AKT2-mTOR Axis Drives Adipose Senescence and Aging-Related Functional Decline
data.authors: He Y; Pan L; Ping W; Meng C; Meng X; Guo Y; Kan R; Xiang Y; Mao B; Wang S; Li D; Yu X

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human cohort (correlation) + mouse (Angptl8-/- knockout, lifespan) + primary adipocyte/cell studies
data.finding: Identifies ANGPTL8 as an endocrine driver of adipose-tissue aging: circulating ANGPTL8 tracked with biological age and mortality risk in a large human cohort, and genetic deletion of Angptl8 in mice extended lifespan and reduced senescence markers. Mechanistically, ANGPTL8 binds AKT2 and drives the AKT-mTOR-S6K axis to promote adipocyte senescence; blocking that axis abolished the pro-senescent effect.

data.title: Long-term treatment with the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin has minor effect on clinical laboratory markers in middle-aged marmosets.
data.authors: Sills AM; Artavia JM; DeRosa BD; Ross CN; Salmon AB

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Middle-aged common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus), daily oral rapamycin, hematology and clinical laboratory markers, sex as a factor
data.finding: In middle-aged marmosets given daily rapamycin, 9 months of treatment produced only minor changes in cellular blood counts, so hematological side effects are not likely outcomes of long-term rapamycin in relatively healthy middle-aged animals. Trough blood concentrations of rapamycin were significantly lower in females than in males, yet both sexes changed little. At baseline, males and females differed little in morphology or in markers of blood cell counts, metabolism and inflammation. Boundary: healthy middle-aged marmosets, 9 months, hematology and clinical laboratory markers only; it says nothing about efficacy or lifespan, and the abstract does not give the dose or group sizes.

data.title: Genetic dissection of the oncogenic mTOR pathway reveals druggable addiction to translational control via 4EBP-eIF4E
data.authors: Hsieh AC; Costa M; Zollo O; Davis C; Feldman ME; Testa JR; Meyuhas O; Shokat KM; Ruggero D

data.finding: Genetic dissection shows the 4E-BP1-eIF4E axis mediates oncogenic mTOR signalling and is druggable.

data.title: Association of rapamycin treatment with the modulation of purine metabolism, reduced microglial inflammatory responses, improved mitochondrial energy metabolism, and alleviation of fatigue symptoms in ME/CFS subjects: pilot findings from phase-II observational study
data.authors: Brooke Gile, Sarojini Bulbule, Mubaraq A Toriola, Brian T Ruan, Shabnam Marium, Anna Benko, Stephanie Grach, Michael Mueller, Lucinda Bateman, Jennifer Bell, Brayden Yellman, Jon Berner, Bela Chheda, David Kaufman, Gunnar Gottschalk, Avik Roy

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: In an uncontrolled phase-II pilot (no placebo), low-dose rapamycin was associated with reduced fatigue in ME/CFS. In plasma from responders, purine intermediates shifted, consistent with lower IMP dehydrogenase activity in PBMCs. Lab assays suggest that altered purines can impair mitochondrial metabolism and promote microglial inflammation; these links were not measured in patients.

data.title: Insulin activation of Rheb, a mediator of mTOR/S6K/4E-BP signaling, is inhibited by TSC1 and 2
data.authors: Garami A; Zwartkruis FJ; Nobukuni T; Joaquin M; Roccio M; Stocker H; Kozma SC; Hafen E; Bos JL; Thomas G

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Insulin activates Rheb-GTP, inhibited by TSC1/2, positioning Rheb as the direct upstream activator of TOR.

data.title: Strengthening Muscle for Healthy Ageing: Innovative Treatments for Sarcopenia
data.authors: Ancel S; Le Moal E; Wang YX; Blau HM

evidence.label: Review — secondary literature, not a new result
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: A major pharma-facing review (Blau lab, Stanford/Sanford Burnham) surveying emerging drug strategies for sarcopenia — the age-related loss of muscle mass/strength with no approved therapy. Among the pleiotropic mechanisms discussed, mTORC1 inhibitors are highlighted specifically for their ability to restore impaired autophagy in aging muscle, alongside NAD-related molecules, urolithin A, myostatin inhibitors, SARMs, and 15-PGDH ('gerozyme') inhibitors. Useful high-level context for where mTORC1 modulation sits among competing anti-sarcopenia strategies, though it does not itself address dynamic/temporal mTOR activity.

data.title: Control of amino-acid transport by antigen receptors coordinates the metabolic reprogramming essential for T cell differentiation

data.authors: DeYoung MP; Horak P; Sofer A; Sgroi D; Ellisen LW

data.finding: Explains how low oxygen turns mTORC1 off. Growth factors keep TSC2 bound to inhibitory 14-3-3 proteins; under hypoxia REDD1 releases TSC2 from 14-3-3, which frees TSC2 to inhibit mTORC1. REDD1-null cells grew into far larger tumours in mice, and REDD1 was low in a subset of human breast carcinomas (8 of 27). Boundary: cell lines and mouse xenografts under acute hypoxia (hours); the human data are expression correlations only.

data.finding: In 24 young Beagles given a 90-day course of rapamycin, the SGLT2 inhibitor canagliflozin, or dietary restriction, rapamycin produced the broadest shift in blood cytokines of the three, while a separate cross-sectional cohort of 80 Beagles aged 1-11 showed that immune aging in dogs is non-linear and sex-stratified rather than a steady decline. data.title: Testing efficacy of administration of the antiaging drug rapamycin in a nonhuman primate, the common marmoset.
data.authors: Tardif S; Ross C; Bergman P; Fernandez E; Javors M; Salmon AB; Spross J; Strong R; Richardson A
data.journal: The Journals of Gerontology: Series A

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), oral Eudragit-encapsulated rapamycin, short-term (3 weeks) and long-term (14 months) studies
data.finding: First description of dosing, pharmacokinetics, biochemical action and tolerability of rapamycin in the common marmoset. Eudragit-encapsulated rapamycin given orally at roughly 1.0 mg/kg/day gave mean trough blood levels of 5.2 ng/mL (range 1.93-10.73), comparable to rodent studies and within the human therapeutic range. In long-term animals (6 of 8) the phospho-rpS6 to total rpS6 ratio fell after 2 weeks, and rapamycin was detectable in liver and adipose tissue with reduced mTOR signalling there. There was no evidence of clinical anemia, fibrotic lung changes or mouth ulcers, and the death rate in the 14-month study was as expected for the animals' ages. Boundary: small cohort (6 of 8 long-term animals showed the pS6 drop), a 3-week and a 14-month study, pharmacology and tolerability only; no lifespan or healthspan outcome was measured, and nothing here is tested in people.

data.authors: Kelly G; Kataura T; Panek J; Ma G; Salmonowicz H; Davis A; Kendall H; Brookes C; Ayine-Tora DM; Banks P; Nelson G; Dobby L; Pitrez PR; Booth L; Costello L; Richardson GD; Lovat P; Przyborski S; Ferreira L; Greaves L; Szczepanowska K; von Zglinicki T; Miwa S; Brown M; Flagler M; Oblong JE; Bascom CC; Carroll B; Reynisson J; Korolchuk VI

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Primary human cells; senescent and naturally aged cells
data.finding: Healthy primary human cells run a high level of basal mitophagy, started by mitochondrial superoxide and carried out through the PINK1/Parkin pathway with p62 as the selective receptor. That housekeeping shuts down on entry into senescence and in naturally aged cells. Blocking mitophagy in young proliferating cells was by itself enough to trigger the senescence program, and reactivation of mitophagy was necessary for the anti-senescence effect of rapamycin and of NAD precursors, which places part of rapamycin's action on cellular ageing downstream of mitochondrial quality control rather than beside it. A p62-targeting small molecule restored mitophagy and rescued markers of cellular ageing.

data.title: ULK1 induces autophagy by phosphorylating Beclin-1 and activating VPS34 lipid kinase
data.authors: Russell RC; Tian Y; Yuan H; Park HW; Chang YY; Kim J; Kim H; Neufeld TP; Dillin A; Guan KL

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Wild-type, ULK-deficient (ULK1-/- with ULK2 knockdown) and FIP200-/- MEFs; HEK293 and HeLa Beclin-1 knockdown-reconstitution lines; in vitro kinase assays with insect-cell ULK1/ULK2; C. elegans bec-1 S6A transgenic embryos
data.finding: The authors asked how the ULK1 kinase switches on autophagy when amino acids are withdrawn. In mouse fibroblasts, amino-acid starvation raised the lipid-kinase activity of VPS34 complexes that contain ATG14L while lowering other VPS34 complexes, and the activation needed ULK kinase activity (lost in ULK-deficient and FIP200-null cells). ULK1 directly phosphorylated Beclin-1 at serine 14 (serine 15 in human), shown with purified kinase, mass spectrometry and a phospho-specific antibody; the mTOR inhibitor Torin1 or amino-acid withdrawal raised this phosphorylation only in cells with ULK activity. Cells reconstituted with non-phosphorylatable Beclin-1 S14A did not increase autophagosomes on amino-acid starvation, and the matching worm mutant (BEC-1 S6A) failed to fully rescue autophagic clearance in C. elegans embryos. The work provided evidence for a signalling chain from mTORC1 inhibition to ULK1, Beclin-1 and the ATG14L-VPS34 complex. Boundary: Mouse and human cell lines, in vitro kinase assays and C. elegans embryos; the mTOR step relies on Torin1 (which blocks mTORC1 and mTORC2) and amino-acid withdrawal. Not tested in mammalian tissues or in people.

The screen is in vitro in iPSC-derived neurons; no animal or human causal test of these genes in FCD is included. Relevant to the Atlas as an expansion of the upstream regulator set, and because the GDNF-withdrawal result shows the hits uncouple mTOR output from growth-factor input.

data.finding: Mice lacking Tsc1 mainly in glial cells (Tsc1 GFAP conditional knockout) develop glial overgrowth, progressive epilepsy and early death. data.title: Rag GTPases mediate amino acid-dependent recruitment of TFEB and MITF to lysosomes
data.authors: Martina JA; Puertollano R

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human ARPE-19, HeLa, HEK-293T cells; siRNA against Raptor, RagA/B, RagC/D, p18 (LAMTOR1); active/inactive Rag mutants; TFEB and MITF deletion/point mutants; Torin1 and amino-acid starvation
data.finding: The authors asked how TFEB reaches the lysosome, where mTORC1 phosphorylates it. In human cells, depleting Raptor inactivated mTORC1 and sent TFEB to the nucleus but did not stop TFEB binding lysosomes (82.5% of cells still showed lysosomal TFEB), whereas depleting the Rag GTPases or the Ragulator subunit p18 abolished it (under 4% of Rag-depleted cells kept the S211A mutant on lysosomes, against about 80% of controls). TFEB bound only active Rag heterodimers through its first 30 amino acids, and active Rags were enough to bring TFEB to lysosomes; TFEB mutants that could not bind Rags lost S211 phosphorylation and stayed in the nucleus. Endogenous TFEB accumulated in the nucleus after Torin1 or amino-acid starvation and moved back to the cytosol and lysosomes when amino acids were added again. Some MITF isoforms behaved the same way. Boundary: Human cell lines, mostly with overexpressed or mutant proteins; not tested in tissues or whole animals.

data.title: L-Arginine Modulates T Cell Metabolism and Enhances Survival and Anti-tumor Activity
data.authors: Geiger R; Rieckmann JC; Wolf T; Basso C; Feng Y; Fuhrer T; Kogadeeva M; Picotti P; Meissner F; Mann M; Zamboni N; Sallusto F; Lanzavecchia A

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human primary naive CD4 and CD8 T cells with high-resolution metabolomics, proteomics and limited-proteolysis mass spectrometry, plus CRISPR knockout T-cell clones; mouse HA-TCR transgenic transfers with oral L-arginine, and B16-OVA melanoma with OT-I transfer
data.finding: Tracking metabolites and proteins in activated human T cells, the authors found intracellular L-arginine falls sharply after activation even in 1 mM medium, because uptake and conversion to ornithine, proline and spermidine rise. Raising L-arginine shifted metabolism from glycolysis towards oxidative phosphorylation, increased oxygen consumption and spare respiratory capacity, and produced central-memory-like cells (CCR7 and CD62L high, less IFN-gamma) with greater survival capacity; blocking arginase gave the same survival gain at physiological 150 uM L-arginine. Limited-proteolysis mass spectrometry plus knockout clones identified three nuclear proteins, BAZ1B, PSIP1 and TSN, that sense L-arginine and contribute to the survival programme. In mice, oral L-arginine raised serum levels from about 160 uM to 700 uM and roughly doubled intracellular L-arginine in activated T cells, and L-arginine-treated OT-I cells slowed B16-OVA growth and extended survival. The authors report explicitly that the survival effect was independent of mTOR: L-arginine did not change S6K1 or 4E-BP phosphorylation, and rapamycin, while also improving survival, changed metabolism in an entirely different way. Boundary: mostly human T cells in culture plus mouse transfer and transplantable-tumour models; the dietary arm is a mouse supplementation experiment, not a human trial, and mTOR enters only as a negative control.

data.authors: McCormack FX; Inoue Y; Moss J; Singer LG; Strange C; Nakata K; Barker AF; Chapman JT; Brantly ML; Stocks JM; Brown KK; Lynch JP; Goldberg HJ; Young LR; Kinder BW; Downey GP; Sullivan EJ; Colby TV; McKay RT; Cohen MM; Korbee L; Taveira-DaSilva AM; Lee HS; Krischer JP; Trapnell BC

data.title: Transient rapamycin treatment can increase lifespan and healthspan in middle-aged mice
data.authors: Bitto A; Ito TK; Pineda VV; LeTexier NJ; Huang HZ; Sutlief E; Tung H; Vizzini N; Chen B; Smith K; Meza D; Yajima M; Beyer RP; Kerr KF; Davis DJ; Gillespie CH; Snyder JM; Treuting PM; Kaeberlein M

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Mice got rapamycin for only 3 months, starting at 20 to 21 months of age, and were then taken off it. A high injected dose (8 mg/kg a day) raised the males' remaining life expectancy after treatment by 60% (p = 0.02), which is a 16% longer median lifespan counted from birth. In females the same dose did not extend life (p = 0.26), and all 16 treated females examined had aggressive blood-cell tumours of the lymphoma type, against 6 of 12 controls, while other tumour types became rarer. A lower dose in the diet (126 ppm; the injected dose was estimated to equal about 378 ppm) raised post-treatment life expectancy by 42% in both sexes together and median lifespan by 13%, improved grip strength and rotarod performance, and changed the gut bacteria (more segmented filamentous bacteria). Boundary: mice only. The tumour counts come from small groups (12 to 16 per arm), side effects such as cataracts or testis changes were not tested at the dietary dose, and 'life expectancy' is counted from the end of treatment, so it makes the gain look larger than the change in total lifespan.

data.title: Rapamycin-induced insulin resistance is mediated by mTORC2 loss and uncoupled from longevity
data.authors: Lamming DW; Ye L; Katajisto P; Goncalves MD; Saitoh M; Stevens DM; Davis JG; Salmon AB; Richardson A; Ahima RS; Guertin DA; Sabatini DM; Baur JA

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality
