data.finding: Chronic rapamycin (about 2 mg/kg a day, close to the lifespan-extending dose) made mice glucose intolerant and insulin resistant. A clamp test placed the problem in the liver, which kept making glucose, while muscle and fat took up glucose normally. Removing mTORC1 from the liver did not cause this. Rapamycin did break up mTORC2 (it separated mTOR from Rictor) in liver, fat and muscle, and deleting Rictor in the liver alone reproduced the glucose problem. In the genetic part, female mice with one working copy each of mTOR and mLST8 had about 50% less mTORC1 signalling in the liver, normal mTORC2 signalling and normal glucose tolerance, and lived 14.4% longer on average (p = 0.046). Males did not. Boundary: mouse drug and genetics work, not people, and the lifespan gain is female-only. It supports separating the two effects, but the paper does not test a drug that blocks mTORC1 without touching mTORC2.

data.title: Health Effects of Long-Term Rapamycin Treatment: The Impact on Mouse Health of Enteric Rapamycin Treatment from Four Months of Age throughout Life
data.authors: Fischer KE; Gelfond JA; Soto VY; Han C; Someya S; Richardson A; Austad SN

data.model_system: Male and female C57BL/6J mice fed microencapsulated rapamycin (14 ppm) or empty capsules from 4 months of age until death (40 per sex per group); repeated longitudinal health assessments from 16 months
data.finding: Mice of both sexes were fed rapamycin in their food (14 ppm, encapsulated) from 4 months of age until death, 40 per sex per group, and the same animals were tested repeatedly for health measures from 16 months of age. Some measures improved: females had stronger grip at all ages, females kept body mass and fat longer during late-life weight loss, and sleep fragmentation fell in males (with a trend in females). Others did not change, such as stride length and age-related cochlear damage, and male rotarod performance was worse. In body mass, percent fat and resting metabolic rate, rapamycin moved males and females in opposite directions. The study showed that lifelong rapamycin in mice affects healthspan measures in a mixed and strongly sex-specific way rather than improving health across the board. Boundary: C57BL/6J mice only, one dietary dose; survival was reported in a companion paper, not in this one, and mTOR activity was not measured here.

data.finding: Cryo-EM structures of a stabilised GATOR2 cage bound to the leucine sensor Sestrin2 or the arginine sensor CASTOR1, plus a structure of leucine-free (apo) Sestrin2, a form that had not been resolved before. The two sensors sit on separate, non-overlapping sites on GATOR2, and mutating those sites selectively blunts mTORC1's response to one amino acid but not the other. When leucine or arginine binds, each sensor changes shape and lets go of GATOR2; while a sensor is attached it holds the mobile WDR24 beta-propeller of GATOR2 in place, a domain needed for nutrient-dependent mTORC1 activation. This shows physically how 'amino acid present' is passed to GATOR2. Boundary: purified human proteins and HEK293T cells — a structural and biochemical model, not a measurement in animals or people. The authors note that some features seen in the Sestrin2 complex may be induced by GATOR2 binding rather than by loss of leucine.

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure

data.finding: Cryo-EM structure of human GATOR2 bound to the arginine-free state of CASTOR1 (3.89 A overall, 3.02-3.72 A after local refinement). data.finding: Working in fruit flies, the authors showed that Akt directly phosphorylates the Drosophila Tsc2 protein in vitro at two conserved residues, Ser924 and Thr1518. data.authors: Franz DN; Leonard J; Tudor C; Chuck G; Care M; Sethuraman G; Dinopoulos A; Thomas G; Crone KR

evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.title: Structure of the lysosomal mTORC1-TFEB-Rag-Ragulator megacomplex
data.authors: Cui Z; Napolitano G; de Araujo MEG; Esposito A; Monfregola J; Huber LA; Ballabio A; Hurley JH

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: First structural view of how mTORC1 actually reaches TFEB to phosphorylate it: two full Rag-Ragulator complexes present a single TFEB molecule to the mTOR active site, one in the normal Raptor-docking arrangement and a second, non-canonical one that grips TFEB's own first helix. Mutating that grip point drives TFEB straight into the nucleus (turning on autophagy/lysosome genes) without disturbing where mTORC1 itself sits. Explains, at the level of atoms, why TFEB phosphorylation needs the tumour suppressor FLCN and the GDP-loaded state of RagC in a way the authors report for no other mTORC1 substrate. Boundary: cryo-EM of a complex reconstituted from purified human proteins — a static structural snapshot, not a live cell or a real-time measurement.

data.title: Influence of rapamycin on safety and healthspan metrics after one year: PEARL trial results
data.authors: Moel M; Harinath G; Lee V; Nyquist A; Morgan SL; Isman A; Zalzala S

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: The authors describe PEARL as the longest trial of rapamycin for healthy ageing so far: 48 weeks, once a week, ages 50 to 85, 114 people finished (40 on 5 mg, 35 on 10 mg, 39 on placebo). The question the trial was built to answer was visceral fat on a DXA scan, and that did not change. Most of what gets quoted comes from secondary results. Lean mass rose in women on 10 mg, and these women also reported less pain, but pain came from a questionnaire the authors did not list as an endpoint, and only eight women were in the 10 mg group, hence the very wide interval (odds ratio 28, 95% CI 2.4 to 324). Side effects were similar to placebo, with more stomach complaints on rapamycin. Bone density was the one signal pointing the wrong way: in the 5 mg group the odds of an improvement in bone mineral density were lower than on placebo (odds ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.93, p = 0.04), but 10 mg showed no change (odds ratio 1.00) and the comparisons between groups were not significant. Boundary: the capsules were compounded, and the authors found they reached about a third of the blood level of the commercial drug, so 10 mg here is closer to 3 mg of generic sirolimus. Dosing was self-reported, and the group was about two thirds men and health-conscious.

data.title: Adjunctive everolimus therapy for treatment-resistant focal-onset seizures associated with tuberous sclerosis (EXIST-3): a phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study
data.authors: French JA; Lawson JA; Yapici Z; Ikeda H; Polster T; Nabbout R; Curatolo P; de Vries PJ; Dlugos DJ; Berkowitz N; Voi M; Peyrard S; Pelov D; Franz DN

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Humans: 366 patients aged 2-65 with TSC and treatment-resistant focal-onset seizures on 1-3 antiepileptic drugs; phase 3 RCT, placebo vs low-exposure (trough 3-7 ng/mL) vs high-exposure (9-15 ng/mL) everolimus; 99 centres, 25 countries
data.finding: EXIST-3 was a phase 3, double-blind trial in 366 patients aged 2 to 65 with tuberous sclerosis complex and focal seizures that had not responded to standard drugs. They were randomised 1:1:1 to placebo (n=119), everolimus dosed to a low blood trough of 3-7 ng/mL (n=117) or a high trough of 9-15 ng/mL (n=130), added to their existing antiepileptic drugs. For the primary endpoint, at least a 50% fall in seizure frequency during the 12-week maintenance period, the response rate was 15.1% with placebo, 28.2% with low exposure (p=0.0077) and 40.0% with high exposure (p<0.0001); median seizure reduction was 14.9%, 29.3% and 39.6%. Grade 3-4 adverse events occurred in 11%, 18% and 24%, and serious adverse events in 3%, 14% and 14% of patients, respectively. The result showed a dose-dependent effect of mTOR inhibition on seizures in TSC, beyond its known effect on TSC tumours. Boundary: patients with TSC and treatment-resistant focal-onset seizures already on 1-3 antiepileptic drugs; comparator was placebo add-on; 18-week core phase (6-week titration, 12-week maintenance), so long-term durability is not addressed here.

data.title: Structure of the human mTOR complex I and its implications for rapamycin inhibition
data.authors: Yip CK; Murata K; Walz T; Sabatini DM; Kang SA

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human mTORC1 purified from HEK-293T cells stably expressing FLAG-raptor; negative-stain and cryo-EM (26 A); antibody labelling; in vitro kinase assays on S6K1 and 4E-BP1 with FKBP12-rapamycin or Torin1
data.finding: The authors purified intact, active human mTORC1 and solved its shape by cryo-electron microscopy at about 26 angstrom resolution. The complex is an obligate dimer with a rhomboid outline and a central cavity, held together by interlocking contacts between mTOR and Raptor; antibody labelling placed mLST8 at the outer 'feet' and PRAS40 next to Raptor. Exposing purified mTORC1 to FKBP12-rapamycin first added a bound density in about 10% of particles, then broke the complex apart, with virtually no intact particles left after one hour, while the ATP-competitive inhibitor Torin1 left it intact. In matching kinase assays, FKBP12-rapamycin blocked S6K1 phosphorylation quickly but 4E-BP1 phosphorylation only after at least 60 minutes, and Raptor-free mTOR still phosphorylated S6K1 (rapamycin-sensitively) but not 4E-BP1. The authors proposed that rapamycin inhibits the two substrates by different mechanisms. Boundary: Purified protein and low-resolution EM; the authors note that in cells rapamycin neither fully blocks 4E-BP1 phosphorylation nor dismantles mTORC1, so the disassembly model is an in vitro result.

data.authors: Facchinetti V; Ouyang W; Wei H; Soto N; Lazorchak A; Gould C; Lowry C; Newton AC; Mao Y; Miao RQ; Sessa WC; Qin J; Zhang P; Su B; Jacinto E

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Cells lacking the mTORC2 components mTOR, SIN1 or rictor lost phosphorylation of Akt and of conventional protein kinase C at the turn motif, a site near the end of the kinase domain. This phosphorylation did not depend on growth factors, and the authors reported the same function in yeast. Turn-motif phosphorylation helped newly made Akt and PKC fold correctly and stay stable; without it, Akt was held by the chaperone Hsp90 and protected from ubiquitin-mediated breakdown. mTORC2 controlled the Akt turn-motif and hydrophobic-motif (Ser473) sites independently in vivo and phosphorylated both directly in vitro. Boundary: Cell culture, yeast and in vitro kinase assays, with mouse tissue for the in vivo site analysis. Shows a protein-maturation role of mTORC2, not an organismal phenotype. Drafted from the abstract only.

data.authors: Yilmaz ÖH; Katajisto P; Lamming DW; Gültekin Y; Bauer-Rowe KE; Sengupta S; Birsoy K; Dursun A; Yilmaz VO; Selig M; Nielsen GP; Mino-Kenudson M; Zukerberg LR; Bhan AK; Deshpande V; Sabatini DM

data.title: Therapeutic reversal of cellular senescence: A systematic review of senolytics, senomorphics and anti-ageing therapies in human clinical trials
data.authors: Trivedi H; Tripathi S; Thacker J; Patil N; Shaikh S

evidence.label: Synthesis of human data
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: A PRISMA-guided systematic review of six completed human clinical studies that met its eligibility criteria, testing drugs that clear or calm senescent ("zombie") cells -- senolytics such as dasatinib+quercetin, plus senomorphic and mTOR-targeting approaches. It reported limited and heterogeneous results, a mixture of biomarker and functional outcomes, with mostly mild side effects, and judged the evidence too thin (small samples, short follow-up) to call any of it an established therapy yet. Six INCLUDED studies is not a census of every completed human senotherapeutic trial: inclusion depends on the review's search date and eligibility criteria, and those have to be stated before any field-wide coverage conclusion is drawn. data.title: Autistic-like behaviour and cerebellar dysfunction in Purkinje cell Tsc1 mutant mice
data.authors: Tsai PT; Hull C; Chu Y; Greene-Colozzi E; Sadowski AR; Leech JM; Steinberg J; Crawley JN; Regehr WG; Sahin M

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: L7Cre;Tsc1 flox mice (Purkinje-cell-specific heterozygous and homozygous Tsc1 deletion); cerebellar slice electrophysiology; behaviour; rapamycin from P7
data.finding: Deleting one or both copies of Tsc1 only in cerebellar Purkinje cells raised phospho-S6 (a readout of mTORC1) in those cells. Both heterozygous and homozygous mutants showed autism-like behaviour: no preference for a mouse over an object or for a new mouse, more self-grooming, more pup ultrasonic calls and poorer reversal learning in a water T-maze. Purkinje cells fired fewer action potentials, both spontaneously and when driven, in a gene-dose-dependent way, while their synaptic inputs looked largely normal; homozygous mutants also lost Purkinje cells from about 2 months of age and became ataxic. Rapamycin (6 mg/kg intraperitoneally, three times a week from postnatal day 7) prevented the Purkinje cell loss and enlargement and the social, learning and motor deficits. Boundary: mouse, cell-type-specific genetic deletion; rapamycin given from early postnatal life, so this is prevention, not reversal; relevance to human autism is by analogy with TSC patients.

data.title: Persistent mTORC1 signaling in cell senescence results from defects in amino acid and growth factor sensing
data.authors: Carroll B; Nelson G; Rabanal-Ruiz Y; Kucheryavenko O; Dunhill-Turner NA; Chesterman CC; Zahari Q; Zhang T; Conduit SE; Mitchell CA; Maddocks ODK; Lovat P; von Zglinicki T; Korolchuk VI

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human fibroblasts made senescent by stress, replicative exhaustion or oncogene activation
data.finding: Explains why mTORC1 stays switched on in senescent cells. In human fibroblasts rendered senescent three different ways, mTORC1 is constitutively active and no longer responds to serum or amino acid withdrawal. The defect is upstream, not in mTORC1 itself: it is driven in part by depolarisation of the senescent plasma membrane, which leads to primary cilia defects and a failure to shut off growth-factor signalling, while increased autophagy and high intracellular amino acid levels may act to support the nutrient arm. Correcting these inputs restored sensitivity of the pathway and killed the cells, which frames persistent mTORC1 signalling as a survival dependency of senescent cells rather than a by-product of senescence.

data.authors: Bonfils G; Jaquenoud M; Bontron S; Ostrowicz C; Ungermann C; De Virgilio C

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Budding yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) genetics and biochemistry; LeuRS Cdc60 and EGO complex (Gtr1) interaction assays
data.finding: In budding yeast, the leucyl-tRNA synthetase Cdc60 bound the Rag GTPase Gtr1, part of the EGO complex that activates TORC1, and this binding depended on leucine. The authors reported that the interaction was both necessary and sufficient to pass the leucine signal on to TORC1. When Cdc60 was busy editing wrongly charged tRNA(Leu), the interaction with Gtr1 was lost. The model is that TORC1 reads how well tRNA(Leu) is being charged as a stand-in for how much leucine the cell has. Together with Han et al. 2012 in human cells, it was one of the early papers to propose a tRNA synthetase as a leucine sensor upstream of the Rags. Boundary: Yeast only. The mammalian leucine sensor most widely accepted today is Sestrin2, and this yeast mechanism has not been reconciled with it. Drafted from the abstract only.

data.authors: Correia-Melo C; Birch J; Fielder E; Rahmatika D; Taylor J; Chapman J; Lagnado A; Carroll BM; Miwa S; Richardson G; Jurk D; Oakley F; Mann J; Mann DA; Korolchuk VI; Passos JF

data.finding: Separates two effects of rapamycin that are usually assumed to travel together. In mice with genetically enhanced NF-kB activity, rapamycin showed no benefit in lifespan and no reduction of inflammaging, yet still reduced frailty and improved long-term memory, neuromuscular coordination and tissue architecture, with lower markers of cellular senescence. data.title: Regulation of the TSC pathway by LKB1: evidence of a molecular link between tuberous sclerosis complex and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
data.authors: Corradetti MN; Inoki K; Bardeesy N; DePinho RA; Guan KL

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: HeLa (LKB1-null) and HEK293 cells; Lkb1-null mouse embryonic fibroblasts; RNAi
data.finding: Asked why two inherited tumour syndromes, tuberous sclerosis and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, look so alike under the microscope. Re-expressing LKB1 in LKB1-null HeLa cells raised AMPK activation-loop phosphorylation and lowered phosphorylation of S6K and 4E-BP1, while knocking LKB1 down did the opposite. The effect on mTOR outputs needed both AMPK and TSC2, placing LKB1 upstream of the TSC2-mTOR axis through AMPK. Together with Shaw et al. 2004 this is one of the two papers that tied energy stress, via LKB1 and AMPK, to TSC2. Boundary: cultured cell lines with overexpression and knockdown; the tumour-syndrome link is an interpretation, not a test in patients.

data.title: Tuberous sclerosis complex-1 and -2 gene products function together to inhibit mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR)-mediated downstream signaling
data.authors: Tee AR; Fingar DC; Manning BD; Kwiatkowski DJ; Cantley LC; Blenis J

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Cultured mammalian cells (HEK293-type transfection system per MeSH 'Cell Line'); coexpression of TSC1/TSC2, patient-derived TSC2 mutant, rapamycin-resistant S6K1 mutants
data.finding: The authors coexpressed hamartin (TSC1) and tuberin (TSC2) in cultured cells and followed two main outputs of mTOR. Together, the two proteins reduced phosphorylation of 4E-BP1, so more 4E-BP1 stayed bound to the translation factor eIF4E; a TSC2 mutant found in TSC patients was defective at this. Hamartin plus tuberin also lowered S6K1 activity, but did not affect S6K1 mutants that resist rapamycin, which points to mTOR as the step being blocked. In nutrient-deprived cells, hamartin and tuberin prevented amino acids from switching S6K1 back on. The authors concluded that the TSC1-TSC2 complex acts as an inhibitor of mTOR signalling and suggested that TSC tumours may come from too much mTOR activity. Boundary: overexpression in cultured mammalian cells; the link to tumours in TSC patients is a proposal, not tested in patient tissue here.

data.title: Rapamycin Exerts Its Geroprotective Effects in the Ageing Human Immune System by Enhancing Resilience Against DNA Damage
data.authors: Kell L; Jones EJ; Gharahdaghi N; Wilkinson DJ; Smith K; Atherton PJ; Simon AK; Cox LS; Alsaleh G

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human T cells (ex vivo, genotoxic stress); ex vivo aged human immune cells; placebo-controlled experimental medicine study in older adults (low-dose oral rapamycin, in vivo)
data.finding: Proposes a geroprotective mechanism for rapamycin that the authors call direct genoprotection. In human T cells exposed to acute genotoxic stress, rapamycin and other mTOR inhibitors suppressed senescence not by slowing protein synthesis, halting cell division, or stimulating autophagy, but by reducing DNA lesion burden and improving cell survival. Ex vivo aged human immune cells showed elevated DNA damage, senescence and mTORC-hyperactivation markers. In a placebo-controlled experimental medicine study, low-dose rapamycin significantly reduced p21 (a DNA-damage-induced senescence marker) in immune cells of older adults versus placebo. Boundary: what was measured is reduced DNA lesion burden under acute genotoxic stress ex vivo, plus one marker (p21) in vivo. 'Genoprotection' as a general property of rapamycin is the authors' interpretation, and no clinical endpoint was measured.

data.title: Reduced dietary protein intake does not alter autophagy in human blood: A randomized crossover study in healthy adults
data.authors: Singh S; Fourrier C; Hein LK; Bensalem J; Martin A; Hattersley KJ; King B; Teong XT; Baker K; Lange K; Barker G; Gore JR; Heilbronn LK; Sargeant TJ

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Randomized crossover trial in healthy adults (n=63 completers, mean age ~29.5y); two 4-week interventions (average-protein 20% energy vs reduced-protein 10% energy) separated by a 4-week washout; autophagic flux measured in whole blood/PBMCs via a validated LC3B-II lysosomal-inhibition flux assay
data.finding: In a rigorous randomized crossover trial, 63 healthy adults completed both a normal-protein (20% energy) and a reduced-protein (10% energy) diet for 4 weeks each. Despite preclinical evidence that dietary protein restriction should activate autophagy via mTORC1 inhibition, directly measured autophagic flux in blood immune cells did not change between the two diets. This is one of the few human studies to test the protein-restriction-to-autophagy link with a dynamic, flux-based (not just steady-state marker) readout, and the negative result suggests that moderate protein reduction alone, without an accompanying caloric deficit, is not sufficient to engage autophagy in humans the way it does in some animal models.

data.title: The mTOR kinase determines effector versus memory CD8+ T cell fate by regulating the expression of transcription factors T-bet and Eomesodermin
data.authors: Rao RR; Li Q; Odunsi K; Shrikant PA

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Naive mouse OT-I CD8 T cells (and STAT4-deficient OT-I) stimulated in vitro with antigen plus B7.1 and IL-12, with rapamycin, PI3K inhibition, insulin or 2-deoxyglucose; adoptive transfer into C57BL/6 recipients and E.G7 tumour challenge
data.finding: Working with naive OT-I CD8 T cells stimulated by antigen plus B7.1, the authors showed that IL-12 both raised and prolonged mTOR phosphorylation and S6K1 Thr389 phosphorylation out to 48 hours, and that this required PI3K throughout and STAT4 for the late phase. Rapamycin, added at the start or only at 12 hours, blocked the sustained expression of T-bet and with it the heritable type I effector programme, while raising Eomesodermin and producing cells with a memory-precursor phenotype (CD62L high, KLRG1 low, Bcl-2 high). After transfer, the rapamycin-treated cells persisted better, gave stronger antigen-recall responses, and more than 78 percent of recipients stayed tumour-free to day 120 against 50 percent fatality with IL-12-conditioned effector cells. Boundary: mouse CD8 T cells, one TCR-transgenic system with pharmacological mTOR inhibition in vitro before transfer; the transplantable E.G7 tumour is a model, not a treatment result in people, and the memory-precursor phenotype faded by day 40 after transfer.

data.authors: Lapp SC; Kalafut KC; Cissé MY; Tighanimine K; Rosenthal DM; Doxsey W; Hui S; Inouye KE; Morrow CE; Cormerais Y; Manning BD

evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Using a mouse model expressing an AKT-nonphosphorylatable TSC2 mutant specifically in skeletal muscle, the Manning lab genetically separated feeding-induced from contraction-induced mTORC1 activation. data.title: Identification of the tuberous sclerosis complex-2 tumor suppressor gene product tuberin as a target of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase/akt pathway
data.authors: Manning BD; Tee AR; Logsdon MN; Blenis J; Cantley LC

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Mammalian cell lines (mouse 3T3 cells, human cells) and PTEN-null tumour-derived cell lines; in vitro kinase assays
data.finding: The authors combined biochemistry with a search for Akt consensus motifs and picked out tuberin, the TSC2 tumour suppressor protein, as a likely Akt substrate. They showed that activating PI3K leads to phosphorylation of tuberin at sites matching the Akt motif, and that Akt can phosphorylate tuberin both in vitro and in cells. Two of these sites, S939 and T1462, were regulated by PI3K, and T1462 stayed phosphorylated in tumour cell lines lacking PTEN. A tuberin mutant without the main PI3K-dependent sites blocked activation of S6K1. Together with papers from other labs in the same months, this was one of the early papers to link growth-factor signalling through Akt to the TSC complex and mTORC1 output. Boundary: cultured mammalian cells and in vitro kinase assays, with overexpressed tuberin mutants; no whole-animal or human tissue data.

data.title: Tuberous sclerosis complex gene products, Tuberin and Hamartin, control mTOR signaling by acting as a GTPase-activating protein complex toward Rheb
data.authors: Tee AR; Manning BD; Roux PP; Cantley LC; Blenis J

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: TSC1-TSC2 acts as a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) for Rheb; when TSC is inactive, Rheb accumulates in its active GTP-bound form and activates mTOR signalling.

data.title: Lysosomal mTORC2/PHLPP1/Akt regulate chaperone-mediated autophagy
data.authors: Arias E; Koga H; Diaz A; Mocholi E; Patel B; Cuervo AM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Mouse liver, rat liver, cell lines (NIH 3T3)
data.finding: Extends the mTOR-autophagy relationship to a third form of autophagy that the Atlas otherwise does not cover, and reverses two of its usual terms. Here it is mTORC2, not mTORC1, that sits on the lysosomal membrane, and it inhibits chaperone-mediated autophagy through Akt, while the phosphatase PHLPP1 counteracts it; the balance controls assembly and disassembly of the translocation complex that pulls single proteins into the lysosome. Boundary: mechanism in cells and rodent liver; the claim that restoring this axis helps in ageing or disease is proposed, not tested here.

data.title: The mTORC1-SLC4A7 axis stimulates bicarbonate import to enhance de novo nucleotide synthesis
data.authors: Ali ES; Lipońska A; O'Hara BP; Amici DR; Torno MD; Gao P; Asara JM; Yap MF; Mendillo ML; Ben-Sahra I

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Building a nucleotide needs a carbon donor, and cells get it from bicarbonate dissolved in their surroundings. This study shows mTORC1 does not just switch on the nucleotide enzymes - it also arranges the delivery of the raw material. Through S6K and the translation factor eIF4B, mTORC1 selectively increases translation of the mRNA for SLC4A7, a sodium-bicarbonate cotransporter, so more bicarbonate is pulled into the cell. Removing SLC4A7 from cells with hyperactive mTORC1 cut flux through both de novo purine and pyrimidine synthesis and slowed cell and tumor growth, without changing intracellular pH - so the transporter matters as a supply line, not as a pH regulator. A fourth distinct route by which mTORC1 feeds nucleotide synthesis, alongside CAD (BEN2013), the mitochondrial folate cycle (BEN2016) and demand coupling (VAL2017).

data.title: Aberrant excitatory neuronal ERBB4 promotes Alzheimer's disease pathology
data.authors: Lee SY; Park E; Lee HE; Kim S; Yeo Y; Park J; Choi YJ; Lee K; Yoon KJ; Park S; Kim E; Kim JI; Chung WS

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Mouse AD models (5xFAD/APP), excitatory-neuron-specific Erbb4 deletion and overexpression; human AD single-nucleus transcriptomics
data.finding: Ectopic ERBB4 in excitatory neurons is one of the earliest changes in AD mouse models and is necessary for synapse loss, reactive gliosis, amyloid plaque deposition and cognitive deficits in AD mice, and its overexpression in wild-type excitatory neurons is sufficient to reproduce synapse loss, gliosis and cognitive deficits (but not amyloid plaques); these effects require mTOR signalling downstream of ERBB4.

data.title: Rapamycin fed late in life extends lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice
data.authors: Harrison DE; Strong R; Sharp ZD; Nelson JF; Astle CM; Flurkey K; Nadon NL; Wilkinson JE; Frenkel K; Carter CS; Pahor M; Javors MA; Fernandez E; Miller RA

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Rapamycin fed from 600 days of age extended median and maximal lifespan in both sexes; age at 90% mortality rose 14% in females and 9% in males.

data.title: A gene network regulating lysosomal biogenesis and function
data.authors: Sardiello M; Palmieri M; di Ronza A; Medina DL; Valenza M; Gennarino VA; Di Malta C; Donaudy F; Embrione V; Polishchuk RS; Banfi S; Parenti G; Cattaneo E; Ballabio A

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Promoter/expression analysis of lysosomal genes; cultured human (HeLa) and mouse cells with TFEB overexpression; lysosomal storage conditions (sucrose loading)
data.finding: The authors found that most lysosomal genes show coordinated expression and share a promoter motif (later called the CLEAR element) that is bound and regulated by the transcription factor TFEB. Under conditions of abnormal lysosomal storage, TFEB moved from the cytoplasm to the nucleus and switched on its target genes. Overexpressing TFEB in cultured cells increased the number of lysosomes and the cells' capacity to degrade complex molecules, including glycosaminoglycans and the mutant huntingtin protein. The paper provided evidence that lysosome production is run by a transcriptional programme with TFEB at its centre, which later work tied to mTORC1 control. Boundary: Cultured cells with TFEB overexpression; mTOR was not studied in this paper. Therapeutic potential for storage and neurodegenerative disease is proposed, not tested. Drafted from the abstract only (no PMC full text).

data.title: Redox activation of ATG5 licenses autophagy upon nutrient restriction
data.authors: Shin S; Korobkina ED; Lennicke C; Burger N; Zhang B; Xiao H; Wang Y; Petrocelli JJ; Wei SM; Wood D; Lei Y; Zhang X; Perez-Matos MC; Sharif MA; Zhang J; Cochemé HM; Mair WB; Chouchani ET

evidence.label: Preprint, not peer-reviewed
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human cell lines and mice; tissue-resolved cysteine redox proteomics (OxiDR atlas) under dietary restriction
data.finding: Dietary restriction selectively oxidizes a specific, tissue-resolved set of cysteines rather than oxidizing the proteome broadly. One of the most strongly oxidized is Cys19 on the core autophagy protein ATG5; this oxidation is required for ATG5 to bind ATG10 and form the ATG5-ATG12 conjugate that lipidates LC3B and builds the autophagosome. In mice lacking this redox switch, nutrient restriction fails to trigger autophagy, causing severe tissue pathology and early death -- a single oxidized cysteine gates the autophagic response to fasting.

data.title: Streptococcus anginosus-associated kynurenic acid drives PD-1 blockade resistance through an ITGA2-mTOR-CTSV axis in gastric cancer.
data.authors: Ren Y; Yu X; Jiang J; Luo J; Zhao C; Mao X; Xi Y; He J; Yu C; Hu Y

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Tumor microbiota-derived kynurenic acid drives resistance to PD-1 blockade in gastric cancer through the ITGA2-mTOR-CTSV axis: kynurenic acid induces ITGA2 and inhibits an mTOR-dependent cascade, which sustains cathepsin V expression and suppresses CD8+ T cell cytotoxic function.

data.title: The LKB1 tumor suppressor negatively regulates mTOR signaling
data.authors: Shaw RJ; Bardeesy N; Manning BD; Lopez L; Kosmatka M; DePinho RA; Cantley LC

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Lkb1-null mouse embryonic fibroblasts; cultured cells under low ATP; gastrointestinal polyps from Lkb1 mutant mice
data.finding: Reported that LKB1 is needed to switch mTOR signalling off when cellular ATP falls, and that this requires AMPK and TSC2. Lkb1-null fibroblasts and the hamartomatous gut polyps of Lkb1 mutant mice showed raised signalling downstream of mTOR. The authors proposed mTOR inhibitors as a treatment idea for Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Published alongside Corradetti et al. 2004, which reached the same LKB1-AMPK-TSC2 link independently. Boundary: worked from the abstract only (no PMC full text); cell and mouse data, the treatment suggestion was not tested here.

data.title: TFEB controls cellular lipid metabolism through a starvation-induced autoregulatory loop
data.authors: Settembre C; De Cegli R; Mansueto G; Saha PK; Vetrini F; Visvikis O; Huynh T; Carissimo A; Palmer D; Klisch TJ; Wollenberg AC; Di Bernardo D; Chan L; Irazoqui JE; Ballabio A

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Mice: 24 h fasting, liver-specific Tfeb knockout, liver-directed TFEB overexpression (helper-dependent adenovirus), high-fat diet and ob/ob obesity, liver Pgc1a and Atg7 deletion, Ppara knockout; HeLa cells, MEFs and primary hepatocytes; C. elegans hlh-30 mutants
data.finding: The authors found that fasting switches on the TFEB gene in mouse liver, muscle and kidney, and that TFEB drives its own transcription by binding CLEAR sites in its promoter, an autoregulatory loop that starvation strengthens. Liver TFEB overexpression changed 773 genes up and 611 down, with lipid catabolism as the top category, and acted largely through PGC-1alpha and PPARalpha: 74% of TFEB-induced genes failed to rise in mice lacking PPARalpha. Mice lacking liver TFEB built up liver fat and mobilised fat poorly during fasting and gained more weight on a high-fat diet, while liver TFEB overexpression prevented and halted diet-induced obesity and improved glucose tolerance in obese ob/ob mice; the lipid effect required autophagy (lost in Atg7-deleted liver). In C. elegans, the TFEB homologue HLH-30 was needed for lipid mobilisation and survival during starvation. Boundary: Mice and worms, with TFEB delivered by virus at overexpression levels. mTORC1 was not manipulated or measured; its role is inferred from earlier work. Not tested in people.

data.title: 4E-BP extends lifespan upon dietary restriction by enhancing mitochondrial activity in Drosophila
data.authors: Zid BM; Rogers AN; Katewa SD; Vargas MA; Kolipinski MC; Lu TA; Benzer S; Kapahi P

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Connected the dots between diet, mTOR, and lifespan. 4E-BP, an mTOR target, is upregulated on dietary restriction and here was shown to be REQUIRED for the lifespan boost, working by selectively boosting translation of mitochondrial genes. A rare case pinning a specific mTOR effector to the longevity benefit of eating less.

data.authors: Jibrin A, Mitchell RT, Lopes F

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure

data.finding: Rapamycin did not protect a mouse spermatogonial cell line from cisplatin damage in vitro, unlike reports in female fertility models.

data.title: AMPK and mTOR regulate autophagy through direct phosphorylation of Ulk1
data.authors: Kim J; Kundu M; Viollet B; Guan KL

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Revealed the tug-of-war over ULK1: the energy sensor AMPK phosphorylates ULK1 at activating sites to turn autophagy ON when energy is low, while mTORC1 phosphorylates a different site (Ser757) to keep it OFF and even blocks AMPK from reaching ULK1. Two opposing kinases wired to the same switch.

data.title: Aberrant Proteostasis of BMAL1 Underlies Circadian Abnormalities in a Paradigmatic mTOR-opathy
data.authors: Lipton JO; Boyle LM; Yuan ED; Hochstrasser KJ; Chifamba FF; Nathan A; Tsai PT; Davis F; Sahin M

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Mouse models of tuberous sclerosis complex (Tsc1/Tsc2 loss)
data.finding: In mouse models of tuberous sclerosis, where mTOR is stuck on, the circadian clock ran abnormally: poor timekeeping in constant conditions and exaggerated responses to phase resetting. mTOR raised BMAL1 levels by changing its translation, degradation and location; genetically lowering BMAL1 rescued the behavioural rhythm defects. Constant, unpatterned mTOR activity disturbs a rhythm downstream.

data.title: High-dose resveratrol supplementation in obese men: an investigator-initiated, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial of substrate metabolism, insulin sensitivity, and body composition
data.authors: Poulsen MM; Vestergaard PF; Clasen BF; Radko Y; Christensen LP; Stødkilde-Jørgensen H; Møller N; Jessen N; Pedersen SB; Jørgensen JO

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.title: mTORC1 supports progression toward activation competence in quiescent adult neural stem cells
data.authors: Thetiot M; Taing L; Morizet D; Letort G; Bally-Cuif L

evidence.label: Preprint, not peer-reviewed
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: In the adult zebrafish brain, mTORC1 activity is enriched during a long quiescence phase in which neural stem cells become able to activate; perturbing mTORC1 changes how cells progress through this phase, setting the tempo of the move towards activation while preserving stemness. Preprint, not peer-reviewed.

data.title: Everolimus plus exemestane for hormone-receptor-positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor-2-negative advanced breast cancer: overall survival results from BOLERO-2†
data.authors: Piccart M; Hortobagyi GN; Campone M; Pritchard KI; Lebrun F; Ito Y; Noguchi S; Perez A; Rugo HS; Deleu I; Burris HA; Provencher L; Neven P; Gnant M; Shtivelband M; Wu C; Fan J; Feng W; Taran T; Baselga J

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Humans: postmenopausal women with HR+/HER2- advanced breast cancer after nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitors; phase III RCT, everolimus + exemestane vs placebo + exemestane (2:1)
data.finding: This is the final overall-survival report of BOLERO-2, the phase III double-blind trial (published primary analysis: BAS2012) in which postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer that had progressed on a nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor received exemestane 25 mg/day plus either everolimus 10 mg/day or placebo. The primary endpoint, progression-free survival by local investigator, remained improved: median 7.8 vs 3.2 months (P < 0.0001), a 4.6-month gain. Overall survival, a key secondary endpoint, was not significantly improved: median 31.0 vs 26.6 months, hazard ratio 0.89 (95% CI 0.73-1.10), P = 0.14, at 410 deaths. Most patients went on to further treatment after the trial (84% vs 90%), with less chemotherapy in the everolimus arm (53% vs 63%), which may have diluted any survival difference. No new safety concerns were identified. Boundary: postmenopausal women with HR+/HER2- advanced breast cancer previously treated with a nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor; comparator was exemestane plus placebo; the survival benefit of adding mTOR inhibition was not shown.

data.title: CASTOR1 regulates humoral immune responses and contributes to the pathogenesis of systemic lupus erythematosus
data.authors: Kusuda T; Komai T; Itamiya T; Abe T; Okamura T; Fujio K

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human B cells (ImmuNexUT transcriptomes, n=136 SLE patients) + whole-body and B cell-specific Castor1-knockout mice
data.finding: Gives the arginine sensor CASTOR1 a defined physiological job upstream of mTORC1: losing it de-represses mTORC1 in B cells and drives plasma-cell expansion, IgG and anti-dsDNA autoantibodies, and lupus-like glomerulonephritis. In human SLE, CASTOR1 expression in plasmablasts was inversely correlated with disease activity (r = -0.32, p = 0.00031). One of the few studies to tie a specific upstream amino-acid sensor to a human autoimmune phenotype rather than to cancer or growth.

data.title: Pharmaceutical inhibition of mTOR in the common marmoset: effect of rapamycin on regulators of proteostasis in a non-human primate.
data.authors: Lelegren M; Liu Y; Ross C; Tardif S; Salmon AB

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), oral rapamycin, liver, skeletal muscle and adipose tissue from a pilot cohort
data.finding: In liver and skeletal muscle from rapamycin-treated marmosets (the earlier pilot cohort), rapamycin was associated with higher expression of PSMB5, a core 20S proteasome subunit, in both tissues but not of PSMB8; proteasome activity itself did not change. Mitochondria-targeted chaperones rose in skeletal muscle but not liver, and autophagy rose in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue but not liver. The authors conclude that only some components of the proteostasis network were upregulated, and in a tissue-specific way. Boundary: tissue samples from a small pilot cohort; the changes are expression-level associations and are not shown to cause any health or lifespan effect.

data.title: Phosphorylation and functional inactivation of TSC2 by Erk implications for tuberous sclerosis and cancer pathogenesis
data.authors: Ma L; Chen Z; Erdjument-Bromage H; Tempst P; Pandolfi PP

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: The MAPK input to mTORC1. In mammalian cells, ERK phosphorylates TSC2 and inactivates the TSC complex, so growth signalling through Ras/ERK converges on the same brake that Akt releases. This is the third major upstream arm alongside PI3K/Akt and AMPK. Its practical significance is that it offers a route to mTORC1 activation that PI3K inhibitors do not close - though that inference is mechanistic; no human data here.

data.title: Everolimus Aging Study (EVERLAST): Clinical Evaluation of mTORC1 Inhibition for Geroprotection
data.authors: University of Wisconsin, Madison (registered trial)

evidence.label: Registered trial, no results yet
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Humans, RCT (registered, completed; no results posted)
data.finding: Phase 2 trial (NCT05835999, EVERLAST) testing this Atlas's open dosing hypothesis directly: whether daily low-dose (0.5 mg/day) or weekly (5 mg/week) everolimus for 24 weeks can improve physiological and molecular hallmarks of aging in insulin-resistant or prediabetic adults aged 55-80, without the metabolic penalty seen with continuous higher-dose rapalog use. Double-blind and placebo-controlled with four arms (everolimus daily, everolimus weekly, and a matching placebo for each), n=106, plus a separate untreated 18-35 cohort for comparison. Primary endpoint is peripheral insulin sensitivity by dual-tracer OGTT; mTORC1 and mTORC2 signalling are secondary endpoints in muscle and blood cells. STATUS: the registry records the trial as COMPLETED, with primary completion 2026-06-30 and completion 2026-07-22. No results are posted yet, so there is nothing to read into the outcome either way.

data.title: 5-Fluorouracil-based chemotherapy disrupts autophagy flux and protein synthesis in cultured myotubes: a role for mTORC1 signaling
data.authors: Halle JL; Zhang Q; Jenkins T; Carson JA

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: C2C12 mouse myotubes (in vitro), with and without CT26 colon-tumor-cell-conditioned media
data.finding: FOLFOX and oxaliplatin disrupted mTORC1/AMPK regulation of autophagy flux and protein synthesis in cultured myotubes; the effect was not easily reversible on drug withdrawal. Rapamycin (but not metformin) restored autophagy flux and AMPK phosphorylation, though without restoring protein synthesis.

data.title: Spalt-related is an inhibitor of mTORC1-mediated growth activated by the integrated stress response
data.authors: Onur Deniz, Ying Liu, Tuuli Kirkinen, Krista Kokki, Kateryna Gaertner, Pau Clavell-Revelles, Jaakko Mattila, Ville Hietakangas

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Transcription factor Spalt-related (Salr) is a novel mTORC1 inhibitor in Drosophila activated by the integrated stress response, restricting anabolic growth and lipid storage during nutrient stress. Salr responds to a distinct, ISR-driven cue, acting convergently with FoxO rather than downstream of it.

data.authors: He L; Cho S; Blenis J

evidence.label: Review — secondary literature, not a new result

data.finding: Comprehensive current review of how nutrients and growth signals are integrated by mTORC1 and the metabolic programs it commands, plus the clinical outlook for mTORC1-targeted therapy across cancer, neurodegeneration, obesity, diabetes and aging -- anchor reference for the pathway map.

data.title: Efficacy and safety of everolimus for subependymal giant cell astrocytomas associated with tuberous sclerosis complex (EXIST-1): a multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial
data.authors: Franz DN; Belousova E; Sparagana S; Bebin EM; Frost M; Kuperman R; Witt O; Kohrman MH; Flamini JR; Wu JY; Curatolo P; de Vries PJ; Whittemore VH; Thiele EA; Ford JP; Shah G; Cauwel H; Lebwohl D; Sahmoud T; Jozwiak S

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Phase 3 RCT (n=117) in tuberous sclerosis, the disease where mTOR is stuck ON by a genetic fault. Everolimus shrank brain tumors (SEGA) by >=50% in 35% of patients versus 0% on placebo. Because the underlying cause here is direct mTOR overactivation, this is arguably the cleanest randomised human evidence that blocking mTOR works in a genetically defined mTORopathy -- which does not extend to mTOR inhibition in people without such a mutation.

data.title: Mathematical Modeling of Dietary Timing- and Protein Quality-Responsive Liver Circadian Clock and its Function on Ribosome Biogenesis
data.authors: Lu L; Levy JL; Anthony TG; Androulakis IP

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Semi-mechanistic computational model of mammalian liver (peripheral clock, mTORC1, GCN2-ISR, ribosome biogenesis)
data.finding: Builds a semi-mechanistic model in which liver mTORC1 and GCN2-ISR signalling are driven by RHYTHMS in dietary essential amino acid availability rather than by a fixed nutrient level. Simulations show the two pathways jointly set metabolic entrainability and are required to keep the peripheral clock and ribosome biogenesis synchronised under nutrient stress, and predict individualised recovery trajectories after a transient dietary disruption. A worked example of treating mTORC1 activity as a time-varying pattern whose shape — not just its average — determines the downstream growth output.

data.title: Distinct perturbation of the translatome by the antidiabetic drug metformin
data.authors: Larsson O; Morita M; Topisirovic I; Alain T; Blouin MJ; Pollak M; Sonenberg N

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human cancer cell line (per MeSH); genome-wide polysome microarray translatome analysis comparing metformin, rapamycin and PP242
data.finding: The authors compared genome-wide changes in mRNA translation caused by metformin with those caused by the mTOR inhibitors rapamycin and PP242 in cancer cells. Metformin changed gene expression at the level of translation to an extent comparable to the classic mTOR inhibitors. Its antiproliferative effect could be explained by selective suppression of translation of mRNAs encoding cell-cycle regulators, acting through the mTORC1 / 4E-BP pathway. The paper provided evidence that metformin's effect on cell growth in vitro goes through selective translational control rather than a general drop in protein synthesis. Boundary: Cultured cancer cells at drug concentrations used in vitro; does not show that metformin at clinical doses acts this way in patients. Drafted from the abstract only.

data.title: DEPTOR is an mTOR inhibitor frequently overexpressed in multiple myeloma cells and required for their survival
data.authors: Peterson TR; Laplante M; Thoreen CC; Sancak Y; Kang SA; Kuehl WM; Gray NS; Sabatini DM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Identified DEPTOR as a built-in brake on BOTH mTOR complexes. The twist: in some multiple myelomas DEPTOR is overexpressed, which by relieving a feedback loop actually keeps pro-survival Akt signaling ON - a neat example of how an 'inhibitor' can be co-opted by cancer.
